The meaning of falah (success) linguistically and in substance has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 181], and all praise is due to God alone.

**The second issue:** God's words, ﴿khāshi'ūn (humble)﴾. Al-Mu'tamir related from Khalid, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to look up at the sky during prayer, so God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse: ﴿those who are humble in their prayer﴾. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began to look at the place where he prostrated." In the narration of Hushaym: "The Muslims used to turn their heads in prayer and look around, until God, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered. Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, so they devoted themselves to their prayer and began to look in front of them."

What the scholars have said regarding the ruling on the one praying who looks toward a certain place has already been discussed in al-Baqarah at God's words: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [see vol. 2, p. 158] [al-Baqarah 2:144]. The meaning of khushū' (humility) linguistically and in substance has also been discussed in al-Baqarah at God's words: ﴿And indeed it is burdensome except for the humble﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 374] [al-Baqarah 2:45]. Humility has its seat in the heart; when the heart is humble, all the limbs become humble on account of its humility, since it is their sovereign, as we have explained at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

When a scholar would establish the prayer and stand to it, he would be in awe of the Most Merciful, avoiding letting his gaze wander to anything or allowing his soul to speak of anything of this world. Ata' said: Humility is not to play with any part of one's body during prayer. The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man fidgeting with his beard during prayer and said: "If this man's heart were humble, his limbs would be humble too."

Abu Dharr said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When one of you stands to pray, mercy faces him, so let him not move the pebbles." Al-Tirmidhi related it.

A poet said:

"Is there not in prayer all goodness and all virtue,
for by it the limbs submit to God in humility?
It is the first obligation of our religion,
and the last thing to remain when religion is lifted."

"Whoever stands for the takbir, mercy meets him,
and he is like a servant knocking at his master's door.
He becomes intimate with the Lord of the Throne at the time of his prayer;
how blessed he is, if only he were humble!"

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni related: It was asked of Aisha, "What was the character of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" She said: "Do you recite Sūrat al-Mu'minūn?" They said, "Yes." She said: "Recite it." So it was recited to her: ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered﴾ until ﴿who guard their prayers﴾.

Al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would glance to his right and left during his prayer, but he would not turn his neck behind his back." Ka'b ibn Malik said in his long hadith: "Then I would pray near him, meaning near the Prophet (ﷺ), and I would secretly glance at him. When I devoted myself to my prayer, he would look at me, and when I turned toward him, he would turn away from me..." [the hadith continues]. He did not order him to repeat the prayer.

**The third issue:** Scholars differed about whether khushū' is one of the obligatory elements of prayer or one of its virtues and completions, on two views. The correct view is the first; its seat is the heart, and it is the first deed to be lifted from the people. This was said by Ubada ibn al-Samit. Al-Tirmidhi related it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', and said: "This is a hasan gharib hadith." Al-Nasa'i also related it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, by a sound chain [in all the manuscripts, the feminine form is used, which is the Hijazi dialect; the masculine form is the dialect of Najd, and the Qur'an came in it]. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: Mu'awiya [one of the narrators of the above hadith] ibn Salih is trustworthy according to the people of hadith, and we know of no one who spoke against him except Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan.

I say: Mu'awiya ibn Salih, Abu 'Amr, also called Abu Umar al-Hadrami al-Himsi, judge of al-Andalus. Abu Hatim al-Razi was asked about him and said: "He is one whose hadith is righteous; his hadith is written down but not used as proof." The statement of Yahya ibn Ma'in about him varied. Ibn Mahdi, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Abu Zur'a al-Razi declared him trustworthy, and Muslim used him as evidence in his Sahih.

The meaning of laghw (idle talk) and zakat has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, so there is no need to repeat it [see vol. 1, p. 343, vol. 3, p. 99].

Al-Dahhak said: Here laghw means shirk (associating others with God). Al-Hasan said: It means all sins. This is a comprehensive statement which includes the view of whoever said it is shirk and the view of whoever said it is singing, as Malik ibn Anas related from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, as will be explained in Luqman [see vol. 14, p. 51 onward].

The meaning of ﴿fā'ilūn (active)﴾ is "those who pay," and it is eloquent Arabic, and it has come in the speech of the Arabs. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"Those who feed the food in the year of drought,
and those who pay the zakat."

**The fourth issue:** God's words, ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾. Ibn al-Arabi said: "It is one of the strange points of the Qur'an that these ten verses are general for men and women, like all the wording of the Qur'an that can apply to both, so they are general to them. Except His words, ﴿and those who guard their private parts﴾, for He addressed men specifically, not wives, as shown by His words, ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾. The fact that a woman guards her private parts is known from other evidence, such as the verses on chastity in general and in particular, and other evidence." I say: On this interpretation of the verse, it is not lawful for a woman to have intercourse with a man she owns, by the consensus of scholars, since she is not included in the verse. But if she frees him after owning him, it is permissible for him to marry her, as it is permissible for anyone else, according to the majority. It was related from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utba, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i that if she frees him at the moment she owns him, the two remain married. Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: No jurist of the regions says this, because in their view her ownership of him annuls the marriage between them, and that is not a divorce but a dissolution of the marriage. And if she frees him after owning him, he cannot take her back except by a new marriage, even if she is still in her waiting period (iddah) from him.

**The fifth issue:** Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam said: I heard Harmala ibn Abd al-Aziz say: I asked Malik about a man who masturbates, and he recited this verse: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ until His words ﴿the transgressors﴾. This is because people use "Umayra" as a euphemism for the penis, and of it the poet says:

"When you dwell in a valley with no one to befriend,
then masturbate, Umayra; there is no disease or sin in it."

The people of Iraq call it istimna' (self-stimulation), which is a derivation from al-maniyy (semen). Ahmad ibn Hanbal, out of his piety, permits it, and argues that it is the expulsion of a residue from the body, so it is permissible when there is need, just as bloodletting and cupping. But the majority of scholars hold it to be forbidden. Some scholars said: It is like one who does it to himself, and it is a sin that Satan introduced and spread among people until it became common, and would that it had never been spoken of. Even if evidence were established for its permissibility, a person of honor would turn away from it because of its baseness. If it is said: It is better than marrying a slave woman, we reply: Marrying a slave woman, even if she is an unbeliever, is better than this according to the view of some scholars, although someone else has also said otherwise. But masturbation is weak in evidence and a disgrace for a base man, so how much more for a noble one?

**The sixth issue:** God's words, ﴿except from their wives﴾. Al-Farra' said: That is, from their wives whom God has made lawful for them, whom they do not go beyond. ﴿Or what their right hands possess﴾ is in the genitive position, conjoined to "their wives," and "mā" is verbal (meaning "what they possess"). This implies the prohibition of adultery (zina) and of what we have mentioned of masturbation and temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah), because the woman in temporary marriage does not take the place of wives: she does not inherit or get inherited from, her child is not attributed to him, and he cannot be separated from her by a divorce that must be initiated for her, but only by the expiry of the term agreed upon, and she is like one who is hired.

Ibn al-Arabi said: If we say that temporary marriage is lawful, then she is a wife for a fixed term, to whom the name of wife applies. But if we hold the truth on which the community has agreed, that temporary marriage is forbidden, she is not a wife and is not included in the verse.

I say: The benefit of this disagreement is whether the prescribed punishment (hadd) is obligatory and the child is not attributed to the man, as in clear adultery, or whether the hadd is averted because of doubt and the child is attributed to him. There are two opinions among our companions. Temporary marriage has had various states of permissibility and prohibition. Among them: it was permitted, then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade it at the time of Khaybar, then he permitted it in the battle of the Conquest, then he forbade it afterward. This was stated by Ibn Khuwayz Mandad from our companions and others, and Ibn al-Arabi alluded to it. Its discussion has already been fully covered in al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 129].

**The seventh issue:** God's words, ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors﴾. He called the one who has intercourse with what is not lawful a transgressor (adi), and made the prescribed punishment obligatory for him because of his transgression. The one who commits sodomy (liwat) is a transgressor by the Qur'an and by language, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:166]. As has been mentioned in al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 242 onward], it is therefore obligatory to apply the prescribed punishment to them. This is clear, and there is no dust on it.

Al-Qurtubi said: I say there is room for scrutiny here, unless the person is ignorant or interpreting, even though there is a consensus (ijma') that the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ apply to men and not to women. Ma'mar related from Qatadah that he said: A woman took her male slave as a sexual partner, and this was reported to Umar, so he asked her, "What led you to do that?" She said, "I thought it was lawful for me by ownership of the right hand, just as a woman is lawful to a man by ownership of the right hand." Umar consulted the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about stoning her. They said, "She interpreted the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in other than its intended sense, so there is no stoning for her." Umar said, "Indeed! By Allah, I will never make you lawful to a free man after him." He punished her with that and waived the prescribed penalty (hadd) from her, and he ordered the slave not to approach her.

And from Abu Bakr ibn Abdullah, that he heard his father say: I was present with Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz when a woman came to him with a boy of hers who had reached puberty. She said, "I took him as a sexual partner, but my paternal cousins prevented me from that. I am only in the position of a man who has a slave-girl and has intercourse with her, so forbid my cousins from me." Umar said, "Did you marry before him?" She said, "Yes." He said, "By Allah, were it not for your standing in ignorance, I would stone you with stones. But take him away and sell him to someone who will take him out of her land."

"Wara'a" (ﻭَﺭَاءَ) here means "other than" (siwa), and it is the object of "ibtaghā" (sought). That is, whoever seeks other than wives and the slave-women they own. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, whoever seeks what is beyond that, so the object of the seeking is omitted, and "wara'a" is an adverbial of place (zarf). "Dhalika" is used to point to everything mentioned, whether feminine or masculine.

﴿Then it is those who are the transgressors﴾, that is, those who exceed the limit, from "ʿadā," meaning he exceeded the limit and passed beyond it.

The eighth matter: His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant, and who are watchful over their prayers﴾. The majority recited "li-amanatihim" in the plural, while Ibn Kathir recited it in the singular. "Amanah" and "ʿahd" together encompass everything a person bears of his religion and his worldly affairs, in speech and action. This includes dealings with people, promises and other matters, and the ultimate aim of this is to preserve it and carry it out. "Amanah" is more general than "ʿahd," and every covenant is a trust in what is previously committed to, whether in speech, action or belief.

The ninth matter: The majority recited "ṣalawātihim" (plural), while Hamzah and al-Kisai recited "ṣalātihim" (singular). This singular is a noun of genus, so it has the meaning of the plural. Guarding the prayer means performing it, hastening to it at the beginnings of its times, and completing its bowing and prostration. This has been discussed fully earlier in al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 1, p. 164 onward.]]

Then He said: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾, that is, whoever acts upon what is mentioned in these verses, they are the inheritors, meaning they inherit the dwellings of the people of the Fire in Paradise.

In a report from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, the Exalted, has made for every person a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. As for the believers, they take their dwellings and inherit the dwellings of the disbelievers, and He places the disbelievers in their dwellings in the Fire." Ibn Majah transmitted it with this meaning. Also from Abu Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but has two dwellings: a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. When he dies and enters the Fire, the people of Paradise inherit his dwelling. That is the meaning of His words, ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾." Its chain is sound (sahih).

It is possible that obtaining Paradise is called inheritance because it is obtained by them and not by others, so the term is used figuratively in both respects.

Al-Firdaws is the highest hill of Paradise, its middle and its best part. Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the hadith of al-Rubayyi' bint al-Nadr, the mother of Harithah, and said: "A hadith, hasan sahih." In Sahih Muslim: "So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle of Paradise, the highest of Paradise, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Hibban said: His words (ﷺ), "for it is the middle of Paradise," mean that al-Firdaws is in the centre of the gardens in breadth, and it is the highest of Paradise, meaning in height. All of this confirms the statement of Abu Hurayrah that al-Firdaws is the mountain of Paradise from which the rivers of Paradise gush forth.

Regarding the word, Mujahid said it is Roman (Greek) and was Arabicised. It was also said that it is Persian and was Arabicised, and it was said that it is Abyssinian. If that is established, then it is a point of agreement among the languages. Al-Dahhak said: It is Arabic, and it means the vineyard, and the Arabs call vineyards "faradis."

﴿They therein are abiding﴾, so the feminine pronoun is used in accordance with the meaning of "Paradise."

Sūrat al-Mu'minūn is entirely Meccan, by the consensus of scholars. In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Certainly the believers have prospered. Those who are humble in their prayer. And those who turn away from idle talk. And those who are active in giving zakat (obligatory alms). And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy. But whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors. And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant. And those who guard their prayers. Those are the inheritors, who will inherit Paradise (al-Firdaws); they will abide therein forever.﴾

In al-Tirmidhi, from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), he said: "When revelation descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ), there was a sound heard near his face like the buzzing of bees. Then it passed from him, and he turned toward the qiblah, raised his hands, and said: 'O God, increase us and do not diminish us, honor us and do not humiliate us, give us and do not deprive us, favor us and do not disfavor us.' This was stated by Ibn Khuwayz Mandad from our companions and others, and Ibn al-Arabi alluded to it. Its discussion has already been fully covered in al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 129].

**The seventh issue:** God's words, ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors﴾. He called the one who has intercourse with what is not lawful a transgressor (adi), and made the prescribed punishment obligatory for him because of his transgression. The one who commits sodomy (liwat) is a transgressor by the Qur'an and by language, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:166]. As has been mentioned in al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 242 onward], it is therefore obligatory to apply the prescribed punishment to them. This is clear, and there is no dust on it.

Al-Qurtubi said: I say there is room for scrutiny here, unless the person is ignorant or interpreting, even though there is a consensus (ijma') that the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ apply to men and not to women. Ma'mar related from Qatadah that he said: A woman took her male slave as a sexual partner, and this was reported to Umar, so he asked her, "What led you to do that?" She said, "I thought it was lawful for me by ownership of the right hand, just as a woman is lawful to a man by ownership of the right hand." Umar consulted the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about stoning her. They said, "She interpreted the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in other than its intended sense, so there is no stoning for her." Umar said, "Indeed! By Allah, I will never make you lawful to a free man after him." He punished her with that and waived the prescribed penalty (hadd) from her, and he ordered the slave not to approach her.

And from Abu Bakr ibn Abdullah, that he heard his father say: I was present with Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz when a woman came to him with a boy of hers who had reached puberty. She said, "I took him as a sexual partner, but my paternal cousins prevented me from that. I am only in the position of a man who has a slave-girl and has intercourse with her, so forbid my cousins from me." Umar said, "Did you marry before him?" She said, "Yes." He said, "By Allah, were it not for your standing in ignorance, I would stone you with stones. But take him away and sell him to someone who will take him out of her land."

"Wara'a" (ﻭَﺭَاءَ) here means "other than" (siwa), and it is the object of "ibtaghā" (sought). That is, whoever seeks other than wives and the slave-women they own. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, whoever seeks what is beyond that, so the object of the seeking is omitted, and "wara'a" is an adverbial of place (zarf). "Dhalika" is used to point to everything mentioned, whether feminine or masculine.

﴿Then it is those who are the transgressors﴾, that is, those who exceed the limit, from "ʿadā," meaning he exceeded the limit and passed beyond it.

The eighth matter: His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant, and who are watchful over their prayers﴾. The majority recited "li-amanatihim" in the plural, while Ibn Kathir recited it in the singular. "Amanah" and "ʿahd" together encompass everything a person bears of his religion and his worldly affairs, in speech and action. This includes dealings with people, promises and other matters, and the ultimate aim of this is to preserve it and carry it out. "Amanah" is more general than "ʿahd," and every covenant is a trust in what is previously committed to, whether in speech, action or belief.

Guarding the prayer means performing it, hastening to it at the beginnings of its times, and completing its bowing and prostration. This has been discussed fully earlier in al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 1, p. 164 onward.]]

Then He said: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾, that is, whoever acts upon what is mentioned in these verses, they are the inheritors, meaning they inherit the dwellings of the people of the Fire in Paradise.

In a report from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, the Exalted, has made for every person a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. As for the believers, they take their dwellings and inherit the dwellings of the disbelievers, and He places the disbelievers in their dwellings in the Fire." Ibn Majah transmitted it with this meaning. Also from Abu Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but has two dwellings: a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. When he dies and enters the Fire, the people of Paradise inherit his dwelling. That is the meaning of His words, ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾." Its chain is sound (sahih).

It is possible that obtaining Paradise is called inheritance because it is obtained by them and not by others, so the term is used figuratively in both respects.

Al-Firdaws is the highest hill of Paradise, its middle and its best part. Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the hadith of al-Rubayyi' bint al-Nadr, the mother of Harithah, and said: "A hadith, hasan sahih." In Sahih Muslim: "So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle of Paradise, the highest of Paradise, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Hibban said: His words (ﷺ), "for it is the middle of Paradise," mean that al-Firdaws is in the centre of the gardens in breadth, and it is the highest of Paradise, meaning in height. All of this confirms the statement of Abu Hurayrah that al-Firdaws is the mountain of Paradise from which the rivers of Paradise gush forth.

Regarding the word, Mujahid said it is Roman (Greek) and was Arabicised. It was also said that it is Persian and was Arabicised, and it was said that it is Abyssinian. If that is established, then it is a point of agreement among the languages. Al-Dahhak said: It is Arabic, and it means the vineyard, and the Arabs call vineyards "faradis."

﴿They therein are abiding﴾, so the feminine pronoun is used in accordance with the meaning of "Paradise."

Sūrat al-Mu'minūn is entirely Meccan, by the consensus of scholars. In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Certainly the believers have prospered. Those who are humble in their prayer. And those who turn away from idle talk. And those who are active in giving zakat (obligatory alms). And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy. But whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors. And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant. And those who guard their prayers. Those are the inheritors, who will inherit Paradise (al-Firdaws); they will abide therein forever.﴾

In this passage there are nine issues.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered﴾. Al-Bayhaqi related from the hadith of Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "When God created the Garden of Eden and planted its trees with His own hand, He said to it, 'Speak.' It said, 'Certainly the believers have prospered.'" Al-Nasa'i related from Abd Allah ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: "I was present with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of the Conquest. He prayed facing the direction of the Ka'bah, and he took off his sandals and placed them on his left side. Then he began Sūrat al-Mu'minūn, and when the mention of Moses or Jesus (peace be upon them both) came, he was seized by a cough and bowed in ruku'." Muslim recorded it with the same meaning.

In al-Tirmidhi, from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), he said: "When revelation descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ), there was a sound heard near his face like the buzzing of bees. One day revelation came down upon him, and we remained with him for a while. Then it passed from him, and he turned toward the qiblah, raised his hands, and said: 'O God, increase us and do not diminish us, honor us and do not humiliate us, give us and do not deprive us, favor us and do not disfavor us.' Then he said: 'Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise.' Then he recited: ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered﴾ until he finished ten verses." Ibn al-Arabi declared it sound.

Al-Nahhas said: The meaning of "whoever observes them" is whoever adheres to them and does not contradict what is in them, as you would say, "So-and-so performs his work." Then after these verses the obligations of wudu' (ablution) and hajj (pilgrimage) were revealed, and they were included with them.

Talha ibn Musarrif recited, "Qad ufliha al-mu'minūn" with a damma on the alif, as a passive verb, meaning: "They were kept safe in reward and goodness." The meaning of falah (success) linguistically and in substance has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 181], and all praise is due to God alone.

**The second issue:** God's words, ﴿khāshi'ūn (humble)﴾. Al-Mu'tamir related from Khalid, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to look up at the sky during prayer, so God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse: ﴿those who are humble in their prayer﴾. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began to look at the place where he prostrated." In the narration of Hushaym: "The Muslims used to turn their heads in prayer and look around, until God, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered. Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, so they devoted themselves to their prayer and began to look in front of them."

What the scholars have said regarding the ruling on the one praying who looks toward a certain place has already been discussed in al-Baqarah at God's words: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [see vol. 2, p. 158] [al-Baqarah 2:144]. The meaning of khushū' (humility) linguistically and in substance has also been discussed in al-Baqarah at God's words: ﴿And indeed it is burdensome except for the humble﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 374] [al-Baqarah 2:45]. Humility has its seat in the heart; when the heart is humble, all the limbs become humble on account of its humility, since it is their sovereign, as we have explained at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

When a scholar would establish the prayer and stand to it, he would be in awe of the Most Merciful, avoiding letting his gaze wander to anything or allowing his soul to speak of anything of this world. Ata' said: Humility is not to play with any part of one's body during prayer. The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man fidgeting with his beard during prayer and said: "If this man's heart were humble, his limbs would be humble too."

Abu Dharr said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When one of you stands to pray, mercy faces him, so let him not move the pebbles." Al-Tirmidhi related it.

A poet said:

"Is there not in prayer all goodness and all virtue,
for by it the limbs submit to God in humility?
It is the first obligation of our religion,
and the last thing to remain when religion is lifted."

"Whoever stands for the takbir, mercy meets him,
and he is like a servant knocking at his master's door.
He becomes intimate with the Lord of the Throne at the time of his prayer;
how blessed he is, if only he were humble!"

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni related: It was asked of Aisha, "What was the character of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" She said: "Do you recite Sūrat al-Mu'minūn?" They said, "Yes." She said: "Recite it." So it was recited to her: ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered﴾ until ﴿who guard their prayers﴾.

Al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would glance to his right and left during his prayer, but he would not turn his neck behind his back." Ka'b ibn Malik said in his long hadith: "Then I would pray near him, meaning near the Prophet (ﷺ), and I would secretly glance at him. When I devoted myself to my prayer, he would look at me, and when I turned toward him, he would turn away from me..." [the hadith continues]. He did not order him to repeat the prayer.

The correct view is the first; its seat is the heart, and it is the first deed to be lifted from the people. This was said by Ubada ibn al-Samit. Al-Tirmidhi related it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', and said: "This is a hasan gharib hadith." Al-Nasa'i also related it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, by a sound chain [in all the manuscripts, the feminine form is used, which is the Hijazi dialect; the masculine form is the dialect of Najd, and the Qur'an came in it]. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: Mu'awiya [one of the narrators of the above hadith] ibn Salih is trustworthy according to the people of hadith, and we know of no one who spoke against him except Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan.

I say: Mu'awiya ibn Salih, Abu 'Amr, also called Abu Umar al-Hadrami al-Himsi, judge of al-Andalus. Abu Hatim al-Razi was asked about him and said: "He is one whose hadith is righteous; his hadith is written down but not used as proof." The statement of Yahya ibn Ma'in about him varied. Ibn Mahdi, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Abu Zur'a al-Razi declared him trustworthy, and Muslim used him as evidence in his Sahih.

The meaning of laghw (idle talk) and zakat has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, so there is no need to repeat it [see vol. 1, p. 343, vol. 3, p. 99].

Al-Dahhak said: Here laghw means shirk (associating others with God). Al-Hasan said: It means all sins. This is a comprehensive statement which includes the view of whoever said it is shirk and the view of whoever said it is singing, as Malik ibn Anas related from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, as will be explained in Luqman [see vol. 14, p. 51 onward].

The meaning of ﴿fā'ilūn (active)﴾ is "those who pay," and it is eloquent Arabic, and it has come in the speech of the Arabs. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"Those who feed the food in the year of drought,
and those who pay the zakat."

**The fourth issue:** God's words, ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾. Ibn al-Arabi said: "It is one of the strange points of the Qur'an that these ten verses are general for men and women, like all the wording of the Qur'an that can apply to both, so they are general to them. Except His words, ﴿and those who guard their private parts﴾, for He addressed men specifically, not wives, as shown by His words, ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾. The fact that a woman guards her private parts is known from other evidence, such as the verses on chastity in general and in particular, and other evidence." I say: On this interpretation of the verse, it is not lawful for a woman to have intercourse with a man she owns, by the consensus of scholars, since she is not included in the verse. But if she frees him after owning him, it is permissible for him to marry her, as it is permissible for anyone else, according to the majority. It was related from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utba, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i that if she frees him at the moment she owns him, the two remain married. Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: No jurist of the regions says this, because in their view her ownership of him annuls the marriage between them, and that is not a divorce but a dissolution of the marriage. And if she frees him after owning him, he cannot take her back except by a new marriage, even if she is still in her waiting period (iddah) from him.

**The fifth issue:** Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam said: I heard Harmala ibn Abd al-Aziz say: I asked Malik about a man who masturbates, and he recited this verse: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ until His words ﴿the transgressors﴾. This is because people use "Umayra" as a euphemism for the penis, and of it the poet says:

"When you dwell in a valley with no one to befriend,
then masturbate, Umayra; there is no disease or sin in it."

The people of Iraq call it istimna' (self-stimulation), which is a derivation from al-maniyy (semen). Ahmad ibn Hanbal, out of his piety, permits it, and argues that it is the expulsion of a residue from the body, so it is permissible when there is need, just as bloodletting and cupping. But the majority of scholars hold it to be forbidden. Some scholars said: It is like one who does it to himself, and it is a sin that Satan introduced and spread among people until it became common, and would that it had never been spoken of. Even if evidence were established for its permissibility, a person of honor would turn away from it because of its baseness. If it is said: It is better than marrying a slave woman, we reply: Marrying a slave woman, even if she is an unbeliever, is better than this according to the view of some scholars, although someone else has also said otherwise. But masturbation is weak in evidence and a disgrace for a base man, so how much more for a noble one?

**The sixth issue:** God's words, ﴿except from their wives﴾. Al-Farra' said: That is, from their wives whom God has made lawful for them, whom they do not go beyond. ﴿Or what their right hands possess﴾ is in the genitive position, conjoined to "their wives," and "mā" is verbal (meaning "what they possess"). This implies the prohibition of adultery (zina) and of what we have mentioned of masturbation and temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah), because the woman in temporary marriage does not take the place of wives: she does not inherit or get inherited from, her child is not attributed to him, and he cannot be separated from her by a divorce that must be initiated for her, but only by the expiry of the term agreed upon, and she is like one who is hired.

Ibn al-Arabi said: If we say that temporary marriage is lawful, then she is a wife for a fixed term, to whom the name of wife applies. But if we hold the truth on which the community has agreed, that temporary marriage is forbidden, she is not a wife and is not included in the verse.

I say: The benefit of this disagreement is whether the prescribed punishment (hadd) is obligatory and the child is not attributed to the man, as in clear adultery, or whether the hadd is averted because of doubt and the child is attributed to him. There are two opinions among our companions. Temporary marriage has had various states of permissibility and prohibition. The meaning of khushū' (humility) linguistically and in substance has also been discussed in al-Baqarah at God's words: ﴿And indeed it is burdensome except for the humble﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 374] [al-Baqarah 2:45]. Humility has its seat in the heart; when the heart is humble, all the limbs become humble on account of its humility, since it is their sovereign, as we have explained at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

When a scholar would establish the prayer and stand to it, he would be in awe of the Most Merciful, avoiding letting his gaze wander to anything or allowing his soul to speak of anything of this world. Ata' said: Humility is not to play with any part of one's body during prayer. The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man fidgeting with his beard during prayer and said: "If this man's heart were humble, his limbs would be humble too."

Abu Dharr said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When one of you stands to pray, mercy faces him, so let him not move the pebbles." Al-Tirmidhi related it.

A poet said:

"Is there not in prayer all goodness and all virtue,
for by it the limbs submit to God in humility?
It is the first obligation of our religion,
and the last thing to remain when religion is lifted."

"Whoever stands for the takbir, mercy meets him,
and he is like a servant knocking at his master's door.
He becomes intimate with the Lord of the Throne at the time of his prayer;
how blessed he is, if only he were humble!"

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni related: It was asked of Aisha, "What was the character of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" She said: "Do you recite Sūrat al-Mu'minūn?" They said, "Yes." She said: "Recite it." So it was recited to her: ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered﴾ until ﴿who guard their prayers﴾.

Al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would glance to his right and left during his prayer, but he would not turn his neck behind his back." Ka'b ibn Malik said in his long hadith: "Then I would pray near him, meaning near the Prophet (ﷺ), and I would secretly glance at him. When I devoted myself to my prayer, he would look at me, and when I turned toward him, he would turn away from me..." [the hadith continues]. He did not order him to repeat the prayer.

**The third issue:** Scholars differed about whether khushū' is one of the obligatory elements of prayer or one of its virtues and completions, on two views. The correct view is the first; its seat is the heart, and it is the first deed to be lifted from the people. This was said by Ubada ibn al-Samit. Al-Tirmidhi related it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', and said: "This is a hasan gharib hadith." Al-Nasa'i also related it from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, by a sound chain [in all the manuscripts, the feminine form is used, which is the Hijazi dialect; the masculine form is the dialect of Najd, and the Qur'an came in it]. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: Mu'awiya [one of the narrators of the above hadith] ibn Salih is trustworthy according to the people of hadith, and we know of no one who spoke against him except Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan.

I say: Mu'awiya ibn Salih, Abu 'Amr, also called Abu Umar al-Hadrami al-Himsi, judge of al-Andalus. Abu Hatim al-Razi was asked about him and said: "He is one whose hadith is righteous; his hadith is written down but not used as proof." The statement of Yahya ibn Ma'in about him varied. Ibn Mahdi, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Abu Zur'a al-Razi declared him trustworthy, and Muslim used him as evidence in his Sahih.

The meaning of laghw (idle talk) and zakat has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, so there is no need to repeat it [see vol. 1, p. 343, vol. 3, p. 99].

Al-Dahhak said: Here laghw means shirk (associating others with God). Al-Hasan said: It means all sins. This is a comprehensive statement which includes the view of whoever said it is shirk and the view of whoever said it is singing, as Malik ibn Anas related from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, as will be explained in Luqman [see vol. 14, p. 51 onward].

The meaning of ﴿fā'ilūn (active)﴾ is "those who pay," and it is eloquent Arabic, and it has come in the speech of the Arabs. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"Those who feed the food in the year of drought,
and those who pay the zakat."

**The fourth issue:** God's words, ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾. Ibn al-Arabi said: "It is one of the strange points of the Qur'an that these ten verses are general for men and women, like all the wording of the Qur'an that can apply to both, so they are general to them. Except His words, ﴿and those who guard their private parts﴾, for He addressed men specifically, not wives, as shown by His words, ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾. The fact that a woman guards her private parts is known from other evidence, such as the verses on chastity in general and in particular, and other evidence." I say: On this interpretation of the verse, it is not lawful for a woman to have intercourse with a man she owns, by the consensus of scholars, since she is not included in the verse. But if she frees him after owning him, it is permissible for him to marry her, as it is permissible for anyone else, according to the majority. It was related from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utba, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i that if she frees him at the moment she owns him, the two remain married. Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: No jurist of the regions says this, because in their view her ownership of him annuls the marriage between them, and that is not a divorce but a dissolution of the marriage. And if she frees him after owning him, he cannot take her back except by a new marriage, even if she is still in her waiting period (iddah) from him.

**The fifth issue:** Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam said: I heard Harmala ibn Abd al-Aziz say: I asked Malik about a man who masturbates, and he recited this verse: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ until His words ﴿the transgressors﴾. This is because people use "Umayra" as a euphemism for the penis, and of it the poet says:

"When you dwell in a valley with no one to befriend,
then masturbate, Umayra; there is no disease or sin in it."

The people of Iraq call it istimna' (self-stimulation), which is a derivation from al-maniyy (semen). Ahmad ibn Hanbal, out of his piety, permits it, and argues that it is the expulsion of a residue from the body, so it is permissible when there is need, just as bloodletting and cupping. But the majority of scholars hold it to be forbidden. Some scholars said: It is like one who does it to himself, and it is a sin that Satan introduced and spread among people until it became common, and would that it had never been spoken of. Even if evidence were established for its permissibility, a person of honor would turn away from it because of its baseness. If it is said: It is better than marrying a slave woman, we reply: Marrying a slave woman, even if she is an unbeliever, is better than this according to the view of some scholars, although someone else has also said otherwise. But masturbation is weak in evidence and a disgrace for a base man, so how much more for a noble one?

**The sixth issue:** God's words, ﴿except from their wives﴾. Al-Farra' said: That is, from their wives whom God has made lawful for them, whom they do not go beyond. ﴿Or what their right hands possess﴾ is in the genitive position, conjoined to "their wives," and "mā" is verbal (meaning "what they possess"). This implies the prohibition of adultery (zina) and of what we have mentioned of masturbation and temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah), because the woman in temporary marriage does not take the place of wives: she does not inherit or get inherited from, her child is not attributed to him, and he cannot be separated from her by a divorce that must be initiated for her, but only by the expiry of the term agreed upon, and she is like one who is hired.

Ibn al-Arabi said: If we say that temporary marriage is lawful, then she is a wife for a fixed term, to whom the name of wife applies. But if we hold the truth on which the community has agreed, that temporary marriage is forbidden, she is not a wife and is not included in the verse.

I say: The benefit of this disagreement is whether the prescribed punishment (hadd) is obligatory and the child is not attributed to the man, as in clear adultery, or whether the hadd is averted because of doubt and the child is attributed to him. There are two opinions among our companions. Temporary marriage has had various states of permissibility and prohibition. Among them: it was permitted, then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade it at the time of Khaybar, then he permitted it in the battle of the Conquest, then he forbade it afterward. This was stated by Ibn Khuwayz Mandad from our companions and others, and Ibn al-Arabi alluded to it. Its discussion has already been fully covered in al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 129].

**The seventh issue:** God's words, ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors﴾. He called the one who has intercourse with what is not lawful a transgressor (adi), and made the prescribed punishment obligatory for him because of his transgression. The one who commits sodomy (liwat) is a transgressor by the Qur'an and by language, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:166]. As has been mentioned in al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 242 onward], it is therefore obligatory to apply the prescribed punishment to them. This is clear, and there is no dust on it.

Al-Qurtubi said: I say there is room for scrutiny here, unless the person is ignorant or interpreting, even though there is a consensus (ijma') that the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ apply to men and not to women. Ma'mar related from Qatadah that he said: A woman took her male slave as a sexual partner, and this was reported to Umar, so he asked her, "What led you to do that?" She said, "I thought it was lawful for me by ownership of the right hand, just as a woman is lawful to a man by ownership of the right hand." Umar consulted the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about stoning her. They said, "She interpreted the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in other than its intended sense, so there is no stoning for her." Umar said, "Indeed! By Allah, I will never make you lawful to a free man after him." He punished her with that and waived the prescribed penalty (hadd) from her, and he ordered the slave not to approach her.

And from Abu Bakr ibn Abdullah, that he heard his father say: I was present with Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz when a woman came to him with a boy of hers who had reached puberty. She said, "I took him as a sexual partner, but my paternal cousins prevented me from that. I am only in the position of a man who has a slave-girl and has intercourse with her, so forbid my cousins from me." Umar said, "Did you marry before him?" She said, "Yes." He said, "By Allah, were it not for your standing in ignorance, I would stone you with stones. But take him away and sell him to someone who will take him out of her land."

"Wara'a" (ﻭَﺭَاءَ) here means "other than" (siwa), and it is the object of "ibtaghā" (sought). That is, whoever seeks other than wives and the slave-women they own. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, whoever seeks what is beyond that, so the object of the seeking is omitted, and "wara'a" is an adverbial of place (zarf). "Dhalika" is used to point to everything mentioned, whether feminine or masculine.

﴿Then it is those who are the transgressors﴾, that is, those who exceed the limit, from "ʿadā," meaning he exceeded the limit and passed beyond it.

The eighth matter: His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant, and who are watchful over their prayers﴾. The majority recited "li-amanatihim" in the plural, while Ibn Kathir recited it in the singular. "Amanah" and "ʿahd" together encompass everything a person bears of his religion and his worldly affairs, in speech and action. This includes dealings with people, promises and other matters, and the ultimate aim of this is to preserve it and carry it out. "Amanah" is more general than "ʿahd," and every covenant is a trust in what is previously committed to, whether in speech, action or belief.

The ninth matter: The majority recited "ṣalawātihim" (plural), while Hamzah and al-Kisai recited "ṣalātihim" (singular). This singular is a noun of genus, so it has the meaning of the plural. Guarding the prayer means performing it, hastening to it at the beginnings of its times, and completing its bowing and prostration. This has been discussed fully earlier in al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 1, p. 164 onward.]]

Then He said: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾, that is, whoever acts upon what is mentioned in these verses, they are the inheritors, meaning they inherit the dwellings of the people of the Fire in Paradise.

In a report from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, the Exalted, has made for every person a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. As for the believers, they take their dwellings and inherit the dwellings of the disbelievers, and He places the disbelievers in their dwellings in the Fire." Ibn Majah transmitted it with this meaning. Also from Abu Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but has two dwellings: a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. When he dies and enters the Fire, the people of Paradise inherit his dwelling. That is the meaning of His words, ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾." Its chain is sound (sahih).

It is possible that obtaining Paradise is called inheritance because it is obtained by them and not by others, so the term is used figuratively in both respects.

Al-Firdaws is the highest hill of Paradise, its middle and its best part. Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the hadith of al-Rubayyi' bint al-Nadr, the mother of Harithah, and said: "A hadith, hasan sahih." In Sahih Muslim: "So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle of Paradise, the highest of Paradise, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Hibban said: His words (ﷺ), "for it is the middle of Paradise," mean that al-Firdaws is in the centre of the gardens in breadth, and it is the highest of Paradise, meaning in height. All of this confirms the statement of Abu Hurayrah that al-Firdaws is the mountain of Paradise from which the rivers of Paradise gush forth.

Regarding the word, Mujahid said it is Roman (Greek) and was Arabicised. It was also said that it is Persian and was Arabicised, and it was said that it is Abyssinian. If that is established, then it is a point of agreement among the languages. Al-Dahhak said: It is Arabic, and it means the vineyard, and the Arabs call vineyards "faradis."

﴿They therein are abiding﴾, so the feminine pronoun is used in accordance with the meaning of "Paradise."

Sūrat al-Mu'minūn is entirely Meccan, by the consensus of scholars. In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Certainly the believers have prospered. Those who are humble in their prayer. And those who turn away from idle talk. And those who are active in giving zakat (obligatory alms). And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy. But whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors. And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant. And those who guard their prayers. Those are the inheritors, who will inherit Paradise (al-Firdaws); they will abide therein forever.﴾

In this passage there are nine issues.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered﴾. Al-Bayhaqi related from the hadith of Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "When God created the Garden of Eden and planted its trees with His own hand, He said to it, 'Speak.' It said, 'Certainly the believers have prospered.'" Al-Nasa'i related from Abd Allah ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: "I was present with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of the Conquest. He prayed facing the direction of the Ka'bah, and he took off his sandals and placed them on his left side. Then he began Sūrat al-Mu'minūn, and when the mention of Moses or Jesus (peace be upon them both) came, he was seized by a cough and bowed in ruku'." Muslim recorded it with the same meaning.

In al-Tirmidhi, from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), he said: "When revelation descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ), there was a sound heard near his face like the buzzing of bees. One day revelation came down upon him, and we remained with him for a while. Then it passed from him, and he turned toward the qiblah, raised his hands, and said: 'O God, increase us and do not diminish us, honor us and do not humiliate us, give us and do not deprive us, favor us and do not disfavor us.' Then he said: 'Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise.' Then he recited: ﴿Certainly the believers have prospered﴾ until he finished ten verses." Ibn al-Arabi declared it sound.

Al-Nahhas said: The meaning of "whoever observes them" is whoever adheres to them and does not contradict what is in them, as you would say, "So-and-so performs his work." Then after these verses the obligations of wudu' (ablution) and hajj (pilgrimage) were revealed, and they were included with them.

Talha ibn Musarrif recited, "Qad ufliha al-mu'minūn" with a damma on the alif, as a passive verb, meaning: "They were kept safe in reward and goodness." The meaning of falah (success) linguistically and in substance has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 181], and all praise is due to God alone.

**The second issue:** God's words, ﴿khāshi'ūn (humble)﴾. and the last thing to remain when religion is lifted."

As has been mentioned in al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 242 onward], it is therefore obligatory to apply the prescribed punishment to them. This is clear, and there is no dust on it.

Al-Qurtubi said: I say there is room for scrutiny here, unless the person is ignorant or interpreting, even though there is a consensus (ijma') that the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ apply to men and not to women. Ma'mar related from Qatadah that he said: A woman took her male slave as a sexual partner, and this was reported to Umar, so he asked her, "What led you to do that?" She said, "I thought it was lawful for me by ownership of the right hand, just as a woman is lawful to a man by ownership of the right hand." Umar consulted the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about stoning her. They said, "She interpreted the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in other than its intended sense, so there is no stoning for her." Umar said, "Indeed! By Allah, I will never make you lawful to a free man after him." He punished her with that and waived the prescribed penalty (hadd) from her, and he ordered the slave not to approach her.

And from Abu Bakr ibn Abdullah, that he heard his father say: I was present with Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz when a woman came to him with a boy of hers who had reached puberty. She said, "I took him as a sexual partner, but my paternal cousins prevented me from that. I am only in the position of a man who has a slave-girl and has intercourse with her, so forbid my cousins from me." Umar said, "Did you marry before him?" She said, "Yes." He said, "By Allah, were it not for your standing in ignorance, I would stone you with stones. But take him away and sell him to someone who will take him out of her land."

"Wara'a" (ﻭَﺭَاءَ) here means "other than" (siwa), and it is the object of "ibtaghā" (sought). That is, whoever seeks other than wives and the slave-women they own. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, whoever seeks what is beyond that, so the object of the seeking is omitted, and "wara'a" is an adverbial of place (zarf). "Dhalika" is used to point to everything mentioned, whether feminine or masculine.

﴿Then it is those who are the transgressors﴾, that is, those who exceed the limit, from "ʿadā," meaning he exceeded the limit and passed beyond it.

The eighth matter: His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant, and who are watchful over their prayers﴾. The majority recited "li-amanatihim" in the plural, while Ibn Kathir recited it in the singular. "Amanah" and "ʿahd" together encompass everything a person bears of his religion and his worldly affairs, in speech and action. This includes dealings with people, promises and other matters, and the ultimate aim of this is to preserve it and carry it out. "Amanah" is more general than "ʿahd," and every covenant is a trust in what is previously committed to, whether in speech, action or belief.

The ninth matter: The majority recited "ṣalawātihim" (plural), while Hamzah and al-Kisai recited "ṣalātihim" (singular). This singular is a noun of genus, so it has the meaning of the plural. Guarding the prayer means performing it, hastening to it at the beginnings of its times, and completing its bowing and prostration. This has been discussed fully earlier in al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 1, p. 164 onward.]]

Then He said: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾, that is, whoever acts upon what is mentioned in these verses, they are the inheritors, meaning they inherit the dwellings of the people of the Fire in Paradise.

In a report from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, the Exalted, has made for every person a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. As for the believers, they take their dwellings and inherit the dwellings of the disbelievers, and He places the disbelievers in their dwellings in the Fire." Ibn Majah transmitted it with this meaning. Also from Abu Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but has two dwellings: a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. When he dies and enters the Fire, the people of Paradise inherit his dwelling. That is the meaning of His words, ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾." Its chain is sound (sahih).

It is possible that obtaining Paradise is called inheritance because it is obtained by them and not by others, so the term is used figuratively in both respects.

Al-Firdaws is the highest hill of Paradise, its middle and its best part. Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the hadith of al-Rubayyi' bint al-Nadr, the mother of Harithah, and said: "A hadith, hasan sahih." In Sahih Muslim: "So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle of Paradise, the highest of Paradise, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Hibban said: His words (ﷺ), "for it is the middle of Paradise," mean that al-Firdaws is in the centre of the gardens in breadth, and it is the highest of Paradise, meaning in height. All of this confirms the statement of Abu Hurayrah that al-Firdaws is the mountain of Paradise from which the rivers of Paradise gush forth.

Regarding the word, Mujahid said it is Roman (Greek) and was Arabicised. It was also said that it is Persian and was Arabicised, and it was said that it is Abyssinian. If that is established, then it is a point of agreement among the languages. Al-Dahhak said: It is Arabic, and it means the vineyard, and the Arabs call vineyards "faradis."

﴿They therein are abiding﴾, so the feminine pronoun is used in accordance with the meaning of "Paradise."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 23, verses 12–14:**

There are five issues in this passage.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We created man﴾. "Man" here refers to Adam (peace be upon him), as Qatadah and others said, because he was extracted (*istull*) from clay. The pronoun in His saying "then We made him" (*thumma ja'alnahu*) refers to the son of Adam, although he has not been mentioned, because the matter is well known and the meaning fits only him. A parallel is His saying, "until it was hidden by the veil" (Surah 38:32) [[See vol. 15, p. 195 onward.]]. It was also said that the intended meaning of *sulalah* is the son of Adam, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. On this view, *sulalah* means the choicest of water, meaning the seminal fluid (*al-mani*). *Sulalah* is on the pattern *fu'alah* from *sall*, which is the extraction of one thing from another. One says: "I pulled the hair out of the dough," and "I drew the sword out of the scabbard, and it slid out." From this comes the line:

*"Then draw my garments off your garments, and they will slide away"* [[This is the second half of a line from the Mu'allaqah of Imru' al-Qays. Its first half is: "And if you have been displeased by a disposition of mine."]]

So *al-nutfah* (the drop) is a *sulalah*, and the child is a *salil* and a *sulalah*. By it is meant the water that is drawn out of the loins, drawn out. The poet said:

*"She brought him forth, a sharp-hided, lion-like one, the extracted seed of a womb that was not well guarded"* [[The line is by Hassan ibn Thabit.]]

Another said:

*"Hind is nothing but a well-bred mare, the offspring of noble mares, and a mule covers her"* [[The author of Lisan al-'Arab attributed this line to Hind bint al-Nu'man (under the root s-l-l). *Tajallaluha* means "covers her." As for the word "mule" (*baghl*), Ibn Barri said that some have claimed it is a scribal error and that the correct reading is *nughl* with an "n," meaning the base of people and animals. In the manuscripts B and J it is *tahallaluha* with an unpointed letter, which is the well-known reading.]]

His saying "from clay" (*min tin*) means that the origin is Adam, and he is from clay. I say: that is, from pure clay. As for his offspring, they are from clay and seminal fluid, as we explained at the beginning of Surah al-An'am [[See vol. 6, p. 387.]]. Al-Kalbi said: *sulalah* is the clay which, when you squeeze it, slips out from between your fingers, so what comes out is the *sulalah*.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿a drop﴾ (*nutfah*). The discussion of the drop, the clinging clot, the lump of flesh, and the rulings concerning them has already passed at the beginning of Surah al-Hajj [[See p. 6 of this part.]]. Praise be to Allah for that.

The third: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾. The scholars differed about "another creation." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: it is the breathing of the spirit into him after he had been inanimate. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is his coming forth into this world. Qatadah said, from a group, that it is the growth of his hair. Al-Dahhak said: it is the eruption of the teeth and the growth of hair. Mujahid said: it is the full maturity of his youth, and this is also reported from Ibn 'Umar. The correct view is that it is general: it includes all of this and other things, such as speech, perception, good reasoning, and the acquisition of intelligible knowledge, until he dies.

The fourth: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾. It is reported that when 'Umar ibn al-Khattab heard the beginning of the verse up to His saying "another creation," he said, "So blessed is Allah, the best of creators." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It was revealed thus." In the Musnad of al-Tayalisi it is stated: "The verse 'And We created man from an extract of clay' was revealed, and when it was revealed I said, 'Blessed is Allah, the best of creators,' and then this was revealed: 'So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.'" It is also reported that the one who said it was Mu'adh ibn Jabal. It is also reported that the one who said it was 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, and for this reason he apostatized and said: "I will bring the like of what Muhammad brings." Concerning him was revealed: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed"?﴾ (Surah 6:93). This was explained earlier in al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 39.]].

His saying, ﴿So blessed﴾ (*fatabaraka*) is of the form *tafa'ala* from *al-barakah* (blessing).

(*Ahsan al-khaliqin*, "the best of creators") means the most skilled of artisans. It is said of one who makes something that he "created" it, and from this is the poet's saying:

*"Indeed, you cut what you have created smooth, and some people create but do not smooth"*

Some people went so far as to deny this word for humans, saying that creation is attributed only to Allah, Exalted is He. Ibn Juraij said: He only said "the best of creators" because Allah, Exalted is He, had permitted 'Isa (peace be upon him) to create, and some people were confused about this. The word is not denied of human beings in the sense of making (*al-sun'*); rather, it is denied only in the sense of originating and bringing into existence from nothing.

The fifth [[So in K and Z. In B, J and T: "issue."]]: From this verse, Ibn 'Abbas said to 'Umar when he asked the senior Companions about the Night of Power. They said, "Allah knows best." 'Umar said, "What do you say, O Ibn 'Abbas?" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, Allah, Exalted is He, created seven heavens and seven earths, created the son of Adam from seven things, and made his provision to be in seven things. So I see it on the night of the twenty-seventh." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "Are you incapable [[In al-Durr al-Manthur: "Are you incapable of saying what this boy has said, who has not yet gathered the locks of his head?"]] of bringing the like of what this lad brought, whose head-locks have not yet come together?" This hadith in full is in the Musnad of Ibn Abi Shaybah.

So Ibn 'Abbas meant by "the son of Adam was created from seven" this verse, and by His saying "his provision was placed in seven" the verse: ﴿then We split the earth, splitting it open, and caused to grow in it grain, and grapes and herbage, and olives and palm trees, and enclosed gardens, and fruit and pasture﴾ (Surah 80:26–31) [[See vol. 19, p. 218 onward.]]. Seven of these are for the son of Adam, and the pasture (*abb*) is for the livestock. The herbage (*qadb*) is eaten by the son of Adam, and women grow fat from it. This is one view. It was also said: the herbage is the vegetables, because they are cut (*tuqdab*), so they are the provision of the son of Adam. And it was said: the herbage and the pasture are for the livestock, the remaining six are for the son of Adam, and the seventh is for the livestock, since it is among the greatest of the provisions of the son of Adam.
