Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We created above you seven paths﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: that is, seven heavens. He related from him that it is said: "taraqtu al-shay'" (I placed something), meaning I made some of it upon other parts of it, so the heavens were called ṭarā'iq (paths) because some of them are above others. The Arabs call everything that is above something else a ṭarīqah (path). It was also said: they are called ṭarā'iq because they are the paths of the angels.

﴿And We were never unaware of creation﴾. Some scholars said: that is, unaware of the creation of the heaven. Most of the exegetes said: that is, unaware of all of creation, lest they fall upon them and destroy them. I say: the meaning may also be "And We were never unaware of creation," that is, in attending to their interests and preserving them [[So in K. In B and J it is in the singular.]], and this is the meaning of "the Living, the Self-Subsisting," as has been mentioned before [[See vol. 3, p. 271.]].

The commentary contains four issues.

The first: this verse is among the blessings of God Most High upon His creation, and among the favours He reminds them of. Among the greatest of these favours is water, which is the life of bodies and the growth of living beings. Water sent down from the sky is of two kinds. The first is that which God, glorified and exalted, mentioned and informed that He deposited in the earth, and made stored in it for giving drink to people, who find it when they need it; this is the water of rivers and springs and what is extracted from wells. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others that He meant the four rivers: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile of Egypt, and the Euphrates. Mujahid said: there is no water in the earth except that it comes from the sky. This is not to be taken absolutely, for otherwise salt water exists in the earth, so his statement may be restricted to sweet water. Without doubt God has placed water in the earth and sent down water from the sky. It has been said that His saying, "And We sent down water from the sky," refers to sweet water, and that its origin is from the sea; God, through His subtle kindness and good ordinance, raised it from the sea to the sky until it became pure through that lifting and ascent, then sent it down to the earth so that it could be benefited from. Had the matter been the water of the sea, it could not have been benefited from because of its saltiness.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿with a measure﴾, means in a measure that is beneficial, for if it were abundant it would destroy. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: "And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures, and We do not send it down except in a known measure" [al-Hijr: 21] [[See vol. 10, p. 14.]].

﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾ means the stored water. This is a threat and a warning: in Our power is to remove it and sink it, and people would perish of thirst and their livestock would perish. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: "Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, then who will bring you flowing water?" [al-Mulk: 30] [[See vol. 18, p. 222.]], meaning sunken, disappearing.

The third: al-Nahhas mentioned: it was read to Abu Ya'qub Ishaq ibn Ibrahim ibn Yunus, from Jami' ibn Sawada, who said: Sa'id ibn Sabiq narrated to us, who said: Maslama ibn 'Ali narrated to us, from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down from Paradise to the earth five rivers: Sayhun, which is the river of India; Jayhun, which is the river of Balkh; the Tigris and the Euphrates, which are the two rivers of Iraq; and the Nile, which is the river of Egypt. Allah sent them down from one spring of the springs of Paradise, at the lowest level of its levels, upon the two wings of Jibril, peace be upon him. He deposited them in the mountains, caused them to flow in the earth, and placed in them benefits for people in the kinds of their livelihoods. That is the saying of His, may His praise be exalted: 'And We sent down water from the sky in a measure, and We caused it to settle in the earth.' When the emergence of Gog and Magog approaches, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will send Jibril, and he will lift from the earth the Qur'an, the knowledge, and all five rivers, and that will be raised to the sky. That is His saying: ﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾. When these things are lifted from the earth, its people will have lost the best of religion and of the world."

The fourth: everything that descends from the sky, whether stored or not stored, is pure and purifying; one may bathe with it and perform ablution with it, as will come in explanation in [al-Furqan] [[See vol. 13, p. 39.]].

**The first issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿So We produced﴾, meaning: We made that the means of vegetation, brought it into being through it, and created it. He, may He be exalted, mentioned the date palms and the grapes because they are the fruit of the Hijaz, in al-Ta'if, Medina and elsewhere. This was said by al-Tabari. And because they are also the noblest of fruits, He mentioned them to honour them and to draw attention to them.

﴿For you therein﴾ (10), meaning: in the gardens.

﴿are fruits﴾, other than the fresh dates and the grapes. It may also refer only to the date palms and the grapes, since they have varieties and kinds. The first meaning is more general, covering all fruits.

**The second issue:** If someone swears that he will not eat fruit (*fakiha*), then according to the transmitted position of our school he breaks his oath (*yahnath*, i.e., he breaks the oath and incurs its consequence) by eating green broad beans and similar things. Abu Hanifa said: he does not break his oath by eating cucumbers, *khiyar* (a kind of cucumber), or carrots, because these are vegetables, not fruit. Likewise walnuts, almonds and pistachios, because these things are not counted as fruit.

If he eats apples, peaches, apricots, figs or plums, he breaks his oath. Likewise melon, because all of these are eaten for the enjoyment of fruit, before and after meals, so they are fruit. Likewise the dried forms of these things, except dried melon, because that is eaten only in some regions. He does not break his oath by eating Indian melon, because it is not counted among fruits. If he eats grapes, pomegranates or fresh dates, he does not break his oath. His two companions disagreed and said he does break it, because these things are among the most prized fruits and are eaten for pleasure. The singling out of these in the Book of God, may He be mighty and majestic, is because of the completeness of their meanings, like the singling out of Jibril and Mika'il among the angels.

Abu Hanifa argued by saying: He once joined these things to fruit, saying: ﴿In both of them are fruit and palm and pomegranate﴾ [al-Rahman: 68] [[See vol. 17, p. 185.]], and once He joined fruit to these things, saying: ﴿And fruit and grass﴾ [Abasa: 31] [[See vol. 19, p. 220.]] [Abasa: 31]. The conjoined is other than that to which it is conjoined, and it is not fitting for wisdom to mention one thing with two different terms in a context of favour. Grapes and pomegranates are sufficient in some regions, so they are not fruit. Also, whatever is fruit has no difference between its fresh and dry forms, and dried forms of these things are not counted as fruit, so their fresh forms are likewise not fruit.

There are six issues in this passage.

**The first:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a tree﴾ [23:20]. *Shajaratan* ("a tree") is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with *jannātin* ("gardens"). Al-Farrāʾ permitted the nominative, *wa-shajaratun*, since the verb does not appear, with the sense of "and there is a tree." He means by it the olive tree. It is singled out for mention because of its great benefits in the land of al-Shām, in the Ḥijāz and in other lands, and because it receives little of the care given to other trees, such as watering, digging and the other attentions bestowed on the rest of the trees.

*Takhruju* ("grows forth") is in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah). ﴿That grows out of Mount Sinai﴾ [23:20]. That is, God caused it to grow originally from this mountain, which God has blessed. Ṭūr Sīnāʾ (Mount Sinai) is in the land of al-Shām, and it is the mountain on which God spoke to Mūsā (peace be upon him). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās and others, and it has been discussed earlier in al-Baqarah and al-Aʿrāf [see vol. 3, p. 264; vol. 7, p. 287]. *Ṭūr* means "mountain" in the speech of the Arabs. It has also been said that it is one of the words Arabicised from the speech of non-Arabs. Ibn Zayd said: it is a mountain of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), extending from Egypt to Aylah [Aylah: known today as "al-ʿAqabah"].

There is disagreement concerning *Sīnāʾ*. Qatādah said: its meaning is "the good." According to this interpretation, *al-Ṭūr* must be given tanwīn as a qualifier (naʿt). Mujāhid said: its meaning is "blessed." Maʿmar, on the authority of a group, said: its meaning is "trees," and for them *al-Ṭūr* must also take tanwīn. The majority said: it is the name of the mountain, just as you say "Jabal Uḥud." Also from Mujāhid: Sīnāʾ is a particular stone, and the mountain was attributed to it because it is found there. Muqātil said: every mountain that bears fruit is Sīnāʾ, that is, "good." The Kūfans read the *sīn* with a fatḥah, on the pattern *faʿlāʾ*. The *faʿlāʾ* pattern is common in the speech of the Arabs, and it is not declined (ghayr munṣarif) in definite or indefinite use, because at its end there is the feminine suffix *alif*, which is inseparable from what it is attached to. There is no *faʿlāʾ* in the language (as a pattern) apart from this. Whoever reads *Sīnāʾ* with a kasrah on the *sīn* makes it a *fiʿlāʾ*, and then the *hamzah* in it is like the *hamzah* of *ḥirbāʾ*. It is not declined in this verse because it has been made the name of a place. Al-Akhfash claimed that it is a non-Arabic proper name.

**The second:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yielding oil﴾ [23:20] (*tanbutu bil-duhni*). The majority read *tanbutu* with a fatḥah on the *tāʾ* and a ḍammah on the *bāʾ*, and the implied sense is: it grows along with oil, just as you say, "Zayd went out with his weapon." Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read it with a ḍammah on the *tāʾ* and a kasrah on the *bāʾ*. Scholars differed about the implied meaning on this reading. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the implied meaning is "it produces its fruit, and with it the oil," so the object is omitted. It has also been said: the *bāʾ* is extra (zāʾidah), like His saying: "And do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction" [2:195]. This is the view of Abū ʿUbaydah. A poet said:

*"We strike with the sword and hope for relief."*

Another said:

*"They are free women, not the ones who ride donkeys [or veils],
with black veils, who do not recite the sūrahs."*

[The reading "al-aḥmirah" with the unpointed ḥāʾ is as in the original sources, from the root "s-w-r" with a dotted letter (khāʾ). Al-Khizānah cites it with the undotted ḥāʾ, saying: "al-aḥmirah" is the plural of ḥimār (donkey), with the paucity plural, and donkeys are singled out because they are the basest and worst property. The word has been misread by the dotted khāʾ. He says: "al-akhmirah" is the plural of khimār, which is what a woman covers her head with. See the fifth-hundredth-and-seventh witness in al-Khizānah.]

Abū ʿAlī also said something similar to this, and it has been mentioned before. It has been said: *nabata* and *anbata* have the same meaning, so the sense is as already explained for the majority's reading. This is the view of al-Farrāʾ and Abū Isḥāq, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*"Until, when the herbage had grown (anbata)..."*

Al-Aṣmaʿī denies that *anbata* is used this way, and he doubts the poem of Zuhayr in which it appears:

*"I saw those in need around their dwellings, dwelling there, until, when the herbage grew (anbata)..."*

That is, *nabata*. Al-Zuhrī, al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿraj read *tunbatu bil-duhni* with a ḍammah on the *tāʾ* and a fatḥah on the *bāʾ*. Ibn Jinnī and al-Zajjāj said: the *bāʾ* is the *bāʾ* of circumstance (bāʾ al-ḥāl), meaning "it grows while its oil is with it." In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: *takhruju bil-duhni*, where the *bāʾ* is also the *bāʾ* of circumstance. Ibn Durustawayh said: *al-duhn* is smooth water, and *tunbitu* is from *al-inbāt* (causing to grow). Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh read: *tunbitu* (with a ḍammah on the *tāʾ* and a kasrah on the *bāʾ*), *al-duhnu* (the oil) (with the *bāʾ* omitted and the noun in the accusative). Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and al-Ashhab read: *bil-dihān*.

The purpose of the verse is to enumerate the blessing of olive oil for humans, and it is among the principal blessings that health cannot do without. The meaning of the olive tree includes every oil-bearing tree in all its varieties according to the regions.

**The third:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a condiment for the eaters﴾ [23:20]. This is the reading of the majority. A group read *wa-aṣbāgun* in the plural. ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays read *wa-matāʿan*. By it is meant the oil with which food is dipped (yuṣṭabagh). It is said: *ṣibgh* and *ṣibāgh*, like *dibgh* and *dibāgh*, and *libs* and *libās*. Every relish with which bread is eaten is a *ṣibgh*, as al-Harawī and others have related. The basic meaning of *ṣibgh* is that with which cloth is coloured, and the relish was likened to it because bread is coloured by the *ṣibgh* when it is dipped into it. (In one manuscript: "is coloured" is "is soiled.") Muqātil said: *al-udm* is the olive, and *al-duhn* is the oil. God has placed in this tree both a relish and oil, so on this view the *ṣibgh* is the olive.

**The fourth:** There is no disagreement that everything in which food is dipped, from liquids such as oil, ghee, honey, syrup, vinegar and other sauces, is a relish (idām). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explicitly mentioned vinegar, saying: "What an excellent relish is vinegar." Nine Companions transmitted it: seven men and two women. Among those who transmitted it in the Ṣaḥīḥ are Jābir, ʿĀʾishah, Kharijah, ʿUmar and his son ʿUbayd Allāh, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayrah, Samurah ibn Jundub, Anas and Umm Hāniʾ.

**The fifth:** Scholars differed about what is solid, such as meat, dates, olives and other solid foods. The majority hold that all of these are relish, so whoever swears not to eat any relish and then eats meat or cheese breaks his oath. Abū Ḥanīfah said: he does not break his oath, and his two companions disagreed with him. It is also related from Abū Yūsuf the same view as that of Abū Ḥanīfah. Greens (al-baql) are not a relish according to all of them. Regarding dates, al-Shāfiʿī held two views; the well-known view is that it is not a relish, because of his saying in al-Tanbīh [cf. the reference], and it has been said that he breaks his oath. The sound view is that all of this is relish.

Abū Dāwūd related from Yūsuf ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām who said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) take a piece of barley bread and place a date upon it, and he said: 'This is the relish of this.'" And he (ﷺ) said: "The chief of the relishes of this world and the next is meat." Abū ʿUmar mentioned it. Al-Bukhārī gave a chapter heading "The Chapter on Relish" and related the hadith of ʿĀʾishah. Also, *al-idām* is derived from *al-muʾādamah*, which means agreement, and these things agree with bread, so they are a relish. There is a hadith from him (peace be upon him): "Eat with relish, even if only with water."

Abū Ḥanīfah's argument: the true meaning of a relish is agreement in being eaten together in a manner that does not admit separation, like vinegar, oil and the like. As for meat, eggs and other things, they do not agree with bread but rather exceed it (in the original: "al-mujāwarah"), like melon, dates and grapes. The conclusion: whatever needs to be paired with bread in eating is a relish, and whatever is not needed with bread and is eaten on its own is not a relish. And God knows best.

**The sixth:** al-Tirmidhī related from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may God be pleased with him), who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Eat oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it is from a blessed tree." This is a hadith not known except through ʿAbd al-Razzāq, and he was inconsistent about it: sometimes it is related from ʿUmar from the Prophet (ﷺ), sometimes he related it with doubt, saying: "I think it is from ʿUmar from the Prophet (ﷺ)," and sometimes he said: "From Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Muqātil said: the Ṭūr was singled out with the olive because the first olive tree grew from it. It has also been said: the olive is the first tree to grow in the world after the Flood. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in the livestock there is certainly a lesson for you. We give you drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat. And upon them and upon the ship you are carried.﴾ This was discussed earlier in *al-Nahl* (see vol. 10, pp. 68, 89), and praise be to God. In *Hud* (see vol. 9, p. 30) is the story of the ship and Noah, and the riding of the sea is mentioned in more than one place (see vol. 2, p. 195).

His saying, exalted is He: "upon them" means upon the livestock on land. "Upon the ship" means on the sea. "You are carried" (tuhmalun). Carrying on land is generally done on camels, so the pronoun may refer to some of the livestock. It is related that a man once rode a cow in former times, and God made the cow speak to him. She said: "We were not created for this. We were only created for ploughing."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You have no god other than Him.﴾ It is recited with the genitive (ghayrihi, read as khafd) in agreement with the wording (lafz), and with the nominative (ghayruhu, read as raf') in agreement with the meaning (ma'na). This was already discussed in *al-A'raf* (see vol. 7, p. 233). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is not but a man like you who wants to make himself superior over you﴾, meaning he wants to lead you and be honoured over you by being the one who is followed, while we are his followers.

﴿Had God willed, He would have sent down angels.﴾ That is, had God willed that no one be worshipped besides Him, He would have made His messenger an angel.

﴿We have not heard of this﴾, meaning of the like of his call. It was also said: "We have not heard of the like of him, a human, who brings a message from his Lord."

﴿among our earliest forefathers﴾, meaning among the past nations. Ibn 'Abbas said this. The *ba'* in "bihadha" (with this) is extra, meaning "we have not heard this existing among our earliest forefathers." Then some of them linked to others and said:

﴿He is not but a man in whom is madness﴾, meaning they referred to Noah, "a man with jinnah," that is, insanity, who does not know what he says.

﴿So wait for him for a time﴾, meaning wait for his death. It was also said: wait until his madness becomes evident. Al-Farra' said: "By *hin* (time) here is not meant a specific time; it is like saying: leave him until some day." So when they persisted in their disbelief, he said: ﴿My Lord, support me, for they have denied me﴾, meaning take vengeance on those who did not obey me and did not listen to my message.

﴿So We revealed to him﴾, meaning We sent to him messengers from the sky, ﴿that you build the ship﴾, as its explanation was given earlier.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then put into it﴾, meaning enter into it and place in it. It is said: "salaktuhu fi kadha" and "aslaktuhu fihi" when I made him enter. 'Abd Manaf ibn Rab' al-Hudhali said:

"Until, when they drove them into Qunaidah,
Driving them as the herdsmen drive the scattered camels."
[Qunaidah: a specific place. *Ath-thall* means driving; *ash-sharad* is the plural of *sharud* (scattered).]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you have settled﴾, i.e., have risen up (ʿalawta).

(You and those with you on the ship) riding (it).

(Then say: "Praise be to Allah") i.e., give thanks to Allah for delivering you.

(From the wrongdoing people.) And from drowning. "Al-hamdu lillah" (Praise be to Allah) is the word of every thankful person to Allah. Its explanation has already passed in al-Fatihah [[see vol. 1, p. 131.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 29:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾ The reading of the common (majority of) readers is "munzalan" with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the zay, as a verbal noun (masdar) from al-inzal (causing to descend), meaning: "Cause me to descend a blessed descent." Zirr ibn Hubaysh and Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, and al-Mufaddal read "manzilan" with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the zay, as a place noun (ism al-makan), meaning: "Cause me to descend at a blessed place." Al-Jawhari said: al-manzal (with a fatha on the mim and the zay) is al-nuzul, which is al-hulul (alighting, settling). You say: "nazaltu nuzulan wa manzalan." And he said:

"Did the abode's dwelling-place remind you [of her], a camel-herd, so that you wept, while the flow of the eye's tear was pouring, abundant?"

"Al-manzal" is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun. [[It should be noted that "manzilaha" in the accusative is the second object of "dhakkartuka." "Jamal" is the subject of the verbal noun, which is al-manzal.]] Another person causing it to descend (anzalahu) and asking it to descend (istanzalahu) have the same meaning. And nazzalahu tanzilan; and al-tanzil also means arrangement (tartib). Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: this was when he came out of the ship, like His statement, exalted is He: "Descend in peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations from those with you" [Hud: 48]. It was also said: when he entered it (the ark). According to this, His statement "mubarakan" means with safety and deliverance. I say: In sum, the verse is a teaching from Allah, mighty and majestic, to His servants that when they ride and when they alight they should say this, and even when they enter their houses and greet (one another) they should say it. It is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that whenever he entered the mosque he would say: "O Allah, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."

**The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ [10:67]**, meaning: in the matter of Noah, the ship, and the destruction of the disbelievers. "Signs" means indications of the perfection of Allah the Exalted's power, and that He grants victory to His prophets and destroys their enemies.

(And indeed We were testing) 30. That is, We were only testing the nations before you, meaning We were examining them by sending messengers to them, so that the obedient and the disobedient would become evident and their condition would be made clear to the angels, not that the Lord acquires new knowledge. It was also said: it means We treat them as those who test. This meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 173.]] and elsewhere. It was also said: "in kunna" means "and indeed we had been."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verses 31–32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We brought into being after them﴾, i.e., after the destruction of the people of Noah.

(A generation other [than them]). It has been said: they are the people of ʿAd.

(Then We sent among them a messenger from among themselves), meaning Hud, because no nation was brought into being immediately after the people of Noah except ʿAd. It has also been said: they are the people of Thamud, and (Then We sent among them a messenger) means Salih. They said: the evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He, at the end of the verse: ﴿So the Cry seized them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 41], and its counterpart: "And the Cry seized those who did wrong" [Hud: 67]. [[See vol. 9, p. 59.]]

I say: among those also seized by the Cry were the companions of Madyan, the people of Shu'ayb, so it is not far-fetched that they are the ones meant, and God knows best.

"From among themselves" means from among their own kin, who know his birth and upbringing, so that they would be more inclined to accept his words.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 33–35:

Allah's words: ﴿And the chiefs (al-mala') said﴾, i.e., the nobles, the leaders and the heads.

(Among his people who disbelieved and denied ["bi-ayatina wa liqa'"] the meeting of the Hereafter) meaning the resurrection and the reckoning.

(And We had given them luxury in the life of this world) i.e., We had widened the bounties of this world for them until they became insolent and were brought luxuries (al-turfah), which is like al-tuhfah (gift).

(This is none but a human like you; he eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink) so he has no superiority over you, for he needs food and drink just as you do. Al-Farra' claimed that the meaning of "wa yashrabu mimma tashrabun" is with the omission of "min", i.e., "mimma tashrabuna minhu" (of what you drink from). This is not permitted according to the Basrans, and no omission is needed at all, because "ma" when it is a verbal noun (masdar) does not require a returning pronoun; but if you make it mean "alladhi" (that which), you omit the object and there is no need to supply "min".

(And if you obey a human like yourselves, then you would indeed be losers) meaning: you would be cheated, by abandoning your gods and following him without any superiority he has over you.

(Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?) i.e., raised from your graves. The first "anna" is in the accusative position, as its object is "ya'iduknum" (promises you), and the second is an apposition (badal) to it; this is the view of Sibawayh. The meaning: does he promise you that you will be brought forth when you die? Al-Farra' said: In the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), it is "ayya'iduku idha mitum wa kuntum turaban wa 'izaman annakum mukhrajun", and it is like your saying: "I think if you go out that you are regretful." Al-Farra', al-Jarmi and Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad held that the second "inna" is repeated for emphasis, since the speech was long, so its repetition is good. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "Does he promise you that you, when you die and become dust and bones, your bringing forth will occur?", so the second "inna" is in the nominative position by a hidden verb, as you say: "Today, the fighting" meaning "today the fighting will occur." Abu Ishaq said: it is permissible to read "ayya'iduku annakum idha mitum wa kuntum turaban wa 'izaman annakum mukhrajun", because the meaning of "ayya'iduku" is "ayaqulu innakum" (does he say that you...).

(This is none but a human like you; he eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink) so he has no superiority over you, for he needs food and drink just as you do. Al-Farra' claimed that the meaning of "wa yashrabu mimma tashrabun" is with the omission of "min", i.e., "mimma tashrabuna minhu" (of what you drink from). This is not permitted according to the Basrans, and no omission is needed at all, because "ma" when it is a verbal noun (masdar) does not require a returning pronoun; but if you make it mean "alladhi" (that which), you omit the object and there is no need to supply "min".

(And if you obey a human like yourselves, then you would indeed be losers) meaning: you would be cheated, by abandoning your gods and following him without any superiority he has over you.

(Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?) i.e., raised from your graves. The first "anna" is in the accusative position, as its object is "ya'iduknum" (promises you), and the second is an apposition (badal) to it; this is the view of Sibawayh. The meaning: does he promise you that you will be brought forth when you die? Al-Farra' said: In the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), it is "ayya'iduku idha mitum wa kuntum turaban wa 'izaman annakum mukhrajun", and it is like your saying: "I think if you go out that you are regretful." Al-Farra', al-Jarmi and Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad held that the second "inna" is repeated for emphasis, since the speech was long, so its repetition is good. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "Does he promise you that you, when you die and become dust and bones, your bringing forth will occur?", so the second "inna" is in the nominative position by a hidden verb, as you say: "Today, the fighting" meaning "today the fighting will occur." Abu Ishaq said: it is permissible to read "ayya'iduku annakum idha mitum wa kuntum turaban wa 'izaman annakum mukhrajun", because the meaning of "ayya'iduku" is "ayaqulu innakum" (does he say that you...).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 36:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: It is a word expressing distance, as if they said, "Far is what you are promised," meaning: this does not happen, that which is mentioned of the resurrection (al-baʿth). Abu ʿAli said: It is in the position of a verb, meaning "far has become what you are promised." Ibn al-Anbari said: There are ten dialects (lughat) regarding "haihat" (hayhāt):

- Hayhāta laka (with a fatha on the taʾ), which is the reading of the majority (al-jamaʿa).
- Hayhāti laka (with a kasra on the taʾ), which is related from Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ.
- Hayhātin laka (with a kasra and tanwin), which is related from ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar.
- Hayhātu laka (with a damma on the taʾ), al-Thaʿlabi said: Nasr ibn ʿAsim and Abu al-ʿAliya recited with it.
- Hayhātun laka (with a damma and tanwin), with which Abu Haywa al-Shami recited, as also mentioned by al-Thaʿlabi.
- Hayhātan laka (with a fatha and tanwin). al-Ahwas said:

 "I remembered days that passed of youth, and hayhāta hayhātan, their return to you is far off."

The seventh dialect: ayhāta ayhāta. al-Farraʾ recited:

 "So ayhāta ayhāta is al-ʿAqiq and whoever is in it, and ayhāta a friend by al-ʿAqiq whom we keep company with."

al-Mahdawi said: ʿIsa al-Hamdani recited "hayhāta hayhāta" with sukun (pausal form). Ibn al-Anbari said: Among the Arabs there are those who say "ayhān" with a nun, and among them those who say "ayhā" without a nun. al-Farraʾ recited:

 "Beside me are the ayʿan and the qinʿ entirely, and the concealment of ayhā, how far and remote it is."

These are ten dialects. Whoever says "hayhāta" with a fatha on the taʾ makes it like ayna and kayfa. It has also been said: these are two compound particles, like khamsata ʿashara, Baʿlabakk and Ram Hurmuz, and one pauses on the second with the hāʾ, as you say khamsa ʿashara and sabʿa ʿashara. al-Farraʾ said: its fatha is like the fatha of thamma and rubba, and it is possible that the fatha is an assimilation to the alif and the fatha preceding it. Whoever pronounces it with a kasra makes it like amsi and haʾulaʾ. He said:

 "Hayhāta hayhāta [[In the origins: thus; what is in al-Lisan: hayhāta hayhātan, with fatha and tanwin.]] ilayka rujuʿuha"

al-Kisaʾi said: Whoever pronounces the taʾ with a kasra pauses on it with the hāʾ, saying hayhāh. Whoever pronounces it with a fatha pauses with the taʾ, or if he wishes with the hāʾ. Whoever pronounces it with a damma does so like mundhu, qattu and haythu. Whoever recites "hayhātun" with tanwin, it is a plural which he treats as indefinite (al-tankir), [[In b, j, t and k: al-takthir (multiplication).]] as if he said "buʿdan buʿdan" (far, far). It has also been said: it is genitive and tanwin is added, assimilating it to sounds, as they say ghaqa and taqa. al-Akhfash said: It is permissible for "hayhāt" to be a plural, so the taʾ in it is the feminine plural taʾ. Whoever recites "hayhāta" may have taken it as a declinable noun containing the meaning of distance, and did not make it a noun for a verb so as to make it indeclinable. It has also been said: he likened the taʾ to the plural taʾ, as in His saying, exalted is He: "Then when you pour forth from ʿArafat" [[See vol. 2, p. 413.]] (al-Baqara: 198). al-Farraʾ said: I personally prefer pausing on the taʾ, because among the Arabs there are those who pronounce the taʾ with a kasra in every case, so it is like ʿArafat, Malakut and what resembles them. Mujahid, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla, al-Kisaʾi and Ibn Kathir used to pause on it as "hayhāh" with the hāʾ. It is also related from Abu ʿAmr that he paused on "hayhāt" with the taʾ, and the rest of the readers follow this, because it is a particle (harf). Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever makes the two of them one single word that is not separated from each other, pauses on the second with the hāʾ and does not pause on the first, saying "hayhāt hayhāh," as one says "khamsa ʿashara," as mentioned above. Whoever intends to separate one of them from the other pauses on both of them with the hāʾ and the taʾ, because the original of the hāʾ is taʾ.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is only our life of this world﴾. "Hiya" (it) is a pronoun referring back to "the world" (al-dunya), meaning: life is nothing but what we are in, not the afterlife which you promise us after the resurrection (al-ba'th).

(We die and we live.) It is said: how did they say "we die and we live" when they do not acknowledge resurrection? There are several answers to this. Among them: the meaning is "we are dead (mawat)," that is, we are drops of semen (nutfan), then we live in this world. It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) here, meaning: "It is only our life of this world, in which we live and die," as He said: ﴿And prostrate yourself and bow down﴾ [Al 'Imran: 43]. [[See vol. 4, p. 84 and what follows.]] It was also said: "we die" means the fathers, and "we live" means the children.

(And we will not be resurrected.) That is, after death.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 38–41:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is only a man﴾, meaning the Messenger. ﴿Who has invented (iftara) against Allah a lie﴾, i.e., who has fabricated (ikhtalaqa).

(﴿Against Allah a lie. And we are not going to believe him.﴾ He said, "My Lord, support me, for they have denied me.") This has already been discussed.

(He said, "In just a little while they will surely become regretful.") 40 That is, "ʿamma qalil" means "after a little," and "ma" is an emphatic redundant particle (zaʾidah muʾakkidah).

(They will surely become regretful.) 40 Over their disbelief. The lam is the lam of oath, meaning: "By Allah, they will surely become..."

(So the Shout seized them.) In the exegetical works: Jibril, upon him be peace, cried out at them with a single shout together with the wind through which Allah the Exalted destroyed them, and they all died to the last one.

(And We made them debris like the refuse of a flood.) That is, lifeless and motionless, like the debris (ghuthaʾ) of a torrent, which is what the flood carries of decayed branches, grass and reeds that have dried and crumbled.

(So away with the wrongdoing folk!) That is, destruction for them. It was also said: "Buʿdan" means distance for them from the mercy of Allah, and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Similar to it is "saqyan lahu wa raʿyan" (watering and pasturing for him).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verses 42–44:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We produced after them﴾, meaning: after the destruction of these people.

(Qurunan) meaning: nations.

(Akharin) Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the Children of Israel. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: they denied their prophets, so We destroyed them.

"(Ma tasbiqu min ummatin ajalaha)": "min" is extra (silah), meaning: no nation precedes its appointed time, nor does it delay it, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34]. [[See vol. 7, p. 201.]]

The meaning of (tatra) is "in succession": they follow one another, some after others, as admonition and warning. Al-Asma'i said: "I made my letters follow one another (watartu kutubi 'alayhi), meaning I caused some of them to follow others, except that there is a interval between each one and the next." Others said: al-muwatarah is continuous succession without interval.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "tatrā" with tanwin, as a verbal noun in which tanwin has been added to a fatha on the ra', like your saying "hamdan wa shukran." Stopping on this reading is on the alif that replaces the tanwin. It may also be considered attached to the pattern of Ja'far, so that it is like arta and 'alqa, as the poet said:

yastannu fi 'alqan wa fi mukur

When stopping on this form, imala is permitted, on the intention of stopping on the attached alif. Warsh read between the two pronunciations, like sakra and ghadaba. It is a noun of collective form, like shatta and asra. Its origin is watra, from al-muwatarah and al-tawatur, and the waw was changed to ta', as in al-taqwa, al-tukan, and tijah and similar words. It has also been said that it is from al-watr, which is the single, so the meaning is: We sent them one by one. Al-Nahhas said: On this basis "titra" with a kasra on the first ta' is also permitted, and its position is accusative as a verbal noun, because the meaning of "thumma arsalna" is "watarna" (we made them follow in succession). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial accusative, meaning "successive."

(Fa-atba'na ba'dahum ba'dan) meaning: with destruction.

(Wa ja'alnahum ahadith) the plural of uhdutha, which is what is spoken of, like a'ajib, the plural of u'jubah, which is what is wondered at. Al-Akhfash said: This is only said of evil: "We made them ahadith," and it is not said of good, just as one says: "So-and-so became a hadith," meaning a lesson and a proverb, as He said in another verse: ﴿So We made them ahadith and tore them up completely﴾ [Saba': 19]. [[See vol. 14, p. 290.]] I say: It may also be said "so-and-so is a good hadith" when it is qualified by mention of that, and from it is the saying of Ibn Duraid:

"Indeed a man is but a hadith after him,
so be a good hadith for whoever is mindful."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 49:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾. He means the Torah (al-Tawrah). Moses is singled out for mention because the Torah was revealed to him at Mount Sinai (al-Tur), while Aaron (Harun) was his deputy (khalifah) among his people. And if He had said, "And We certainly gave them both," it would have been permissible [[i.e., outside the Qur'an.]] as He said: "And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion" [Al-Anbiya': 48] [[See vol. 11, p. 295.]].

**The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ (50).** The discussion of it has already passed in *al-Anbiya'* [[See vol. 11, p. 337.]].

(And We gave them refuge on a high ground, a place of settlement and flowing water.) (50) *Al-rabwah* is an elevated place on the earth, and it was discussed earlier in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 3, p. 315.]]. What is meant by it here, according to the view of Abu Hurayrah, is Palestine. He also reported that it is Ramlah [[Ramlah is a great city in Palestine, and it was its capital. It was a fortified frontier post (ribat) for the Muslims.]], and this is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Salam said it is Damascus. Ka'b and Qatadah said it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Ka'b said: "It is the nearest part of the earth to the sky, by eighteen miles." He said:

*"I was lying prostrate under a mound on a high ground,*
*while the south wind and the north wind passed over me in turn."*

Ibn Zayd said it is Egypt. Salim al-Aftas narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning "﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾ (50)": he said, "*al-nashz*" from the earth (a raised ground).

(*Dhat qarar*) (50): that is, level, on which one can settle. It was also said: it has fruits, and for the sake of the fruits the inhabitants settle there.

(And flowing water) (50): clear running water that is visible to the eyes. It is said *ma'in* and *mu'un*, just as it is said *raghif* and *rughuf* (loaf and loaves). This was said by Ali ibn Sulayman. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the water flowing in springs, and on this view the *mim* (in *ma'in*) is an added letter, like its addition in *mabi'* (sold item). Likewise the *mim* is added according to the one who said it is the water that is seen with the eye. It was also said: it is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive). Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is said *ma'ana al-ma'u* when the water flows, so it is *ma'in* and *ma'yun*. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *ma'ana al-ma'u yam'anu mu'unan* when it flows and runs easily, and *am'ana* also, and *am'antuhu*, and *miyah mu'nan* (flowing waters).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 51:

There are three issues in this verse.

The first: The authentic collection (al-Sahih) narrates from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O people, Allah is Good (tayyib) and accepts only what is good, and Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds; indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:51]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:172]." Then he mentioned the man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, who spreads his hands to the sky, saying: "O Lord, O Lord," while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished with the unlawful; so how could his supplication be answered?" [[This sentence is from the words of the narrator, and the pronoun in it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ).]] [[The word "al-rajul" (the man) is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), mentioned in the manner of narration from the words of our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also permissible to read it in the accusative as the object of "dhakara" (he mentioned).]]

The second: Some scholars said: The address in this verse is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he was placed in the position of the messengers, as He said: ﴿Those to whom people said﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:173], meaning Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud. Al-Zajjaj said: This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the plural indicates that all the messengers were commanded thus, i.e., eat of the lawful. Al-Tabari said: The address is to 'Isa (peace be upon him); it is narrated that he used to eat from his mother's spinning. The well-known report about him is that he used to eat from the herbs of the wilderness. The reason for addressing 'Isa with it, as we have mentioned, is to assign it to Muhammad (ﷺ) as an honor to him. It was also said: This statement was addressed to every prophet, because this is their way, which they should follow. So the meaning is: "And We said, O messengers, eat of the good things," just as you say to a merchant: "O merchants, you should avoid usury," so you address him in meaning. It is also connected to this that this statement is suitable for all of their kind; they were never addressed all together, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them all, but each was addressed in his own age. Al-Farra' said: It is like when you say to one man: "Refrain from your harm to us."

The third: Allah the Exalted equated the prophets and the believers in the address concerning the obligation of eating the lawful and avoiding the unlawful. Then He included all of them in the threat contained in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾, may Allah bless His messengers and prophets. If this is the case with them, then what is the assumption of all people about themselves? The discussion of the good things and provision has passed in more than one place [[See vol. 1, p. 177.]], and praise be to Allah. In his words, peace be upon him, "he spreads his hands," there is evidence for the legitimacy of spreading the hands when supplicating toward the sky, and the disagreement and discussion on this has passed, and praise be to Allah [[See vol. 7, pp. 198 and 223.]]. And his words, peace be upon him, "so how could his supplication be answered?" are said in the manner of deeming it unlikely, meaning that he is not worthy of having his supplication answered; but it is permissible that Allah answers him out of His grace, kindness and generosity.

**First issue:** The phrase ﴿وَإِنَّ هذِهِ أُمَّتُكُمْ أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾ means: "And indeed, this your community (ummah) is one community." The meaning is: this which has been mentioned before is your religion and your creed (millah), so hold fast to it. Here "ummah" means religion. Its other senses have been discussed earlier [See vol. 2, p. 127 and vol. 3, p. 30]. From the same usage is the verse ﴿إِنَّا وَجَدْنا آباءَنا عَلى أُمَّةٍ﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 22], meaning "on a religion." al-Nabighah said:

*"I swore an oath, and I left no doubt in your soul; / Would one who holds a religion (ummah) sin while he is obedient?"*

[See vol. 16, p. 74.]

**Second issue:** The reading ﴿وَإِنَّ هذِهِ﴾ is recited with a kasra on the *inna* (إِنَّ) as a new sentence, and also with a fatha on it and a doubled nun. al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) said: it is in a position of nasb (accusative) after the removal of the governing particle, meaning: "I know that this is your religion which I commanded you to believe in." al-Farra' said: *anna* (أَنَّ) is linked to a hidden verb whose implied meaning is: "And know that this is your community." According to Sibawayh, it is linked to the phrase ﴿فَاتَّقُونِ﴾ and the meaning is "So fear Me, because your community is one." This is like the verse ﴿وَأَنَّ الْمَساجِدَ لِلَّهِ فَلا تَدْعُوا مَعَ اللَّهِ أَحَداً﴾ [Al-Jinn: 18], meaning: "because the mosques belong to God, so do not call upon anyone along with God." It is also like the verse ﴿لِإِيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ [Quraysh: 1], meaning: "let them worship the Lord of this House, for the sake of the security of Quraysh." [See vol. 19, p. 19; vol. 20, p. 200.]

**Third issue:** This verse supports the view that the phrase ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الرُّسُلُ﴾ is addressed to all the messengers together, and that they are assumed to be present. If ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الرُّسُلُ﴾ is taken as addressed to Muhammad ﷺ, the connection between this verse and the phrase ﴿فَتَقَطَّعُوا﴾ becomes strained (this is what the copies b, j and k state; the meaning is clear: this assumption makes the link between the two parts unsettled and broken). As for the phrase ﴿وَأَنَا رَبُّكُمْ فَاتَّقُونِ﴾: even if it was said to the prophets, their communities are included in it in meaning, so the connection afterwards is good.

**﴿فَتَقَطَّعُوا﴾** means they split apart, namely the communities: they made their religion into many religions after they had been commanded to unite. Then God mentioned that each of them is pleased with his own opinion and his error, and this is the extreme of misguidance.

**Fourth issue:** This verse relates to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ): "Indeed, those who came before you among the People of the Book split into seventy-two creeds (millah), and indeed this community will split into seventy-three; seventy-two are in the Fire and one is in Paradise, and it is the *al-jama'ah* (the main body of the community)." This was recorded by Abu Dawud, and al-Tirmidhi transmitted it and added: they said, "Who are they, O Messenger of God?" He said, "Those who are upon what I am upon and my companions." He recorded it from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.

This shows that the division warned against in the verse and the hadith concerns the roots of religion and its foundations, because the Prophet ﷺ called them creeds (millal), and informed that holding to any of those creeds leads to entry into the Fire. Such a thing is not said about the branches (furu') of religion, since it does not require counting creeds or punishment in the Fire. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿لِكُلٍّ جَعَلْنا مِنْكُمْ شِرْعَةً وَمِنْهاجاً﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 48]. [See vol. 6, p. 210.]

It was also said that they divided the books, so one group followed the Scrolls (suhuf), another the Torah, another the Psalms (Zabur), and another the Gospel (Injil). **(فَرِحُونَ)** means pleased with it.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 23, verses 55–56:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do they think that what We provide them with of wealth and children﴾. *Ma* (ما) here means *alladhi* (the one which), meaning: Do they think, O Muhammad, that what We give them in this world of wealth and children is a reward for them? It is only *istidraj* (gradual enticement toward ruin) and *imla'* (respite), not hastening them toward good things.

Regarding the predicate (*khabar*) of *inna* (إنّ), there are three opinions. Among them is that it is omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "We hasten for them with it toward good things," and *bihi* (به) was omitted. Hisham al-Darir gave a subtle opinion: he said, "*Anna ma*" (أنّما) is itself the good things, so the meaning becomes "We hasten for them in it," and then he made it explicit and said "*fi al-khayrat*" (في الخيرات), and on this reading there is no omission. The position of al-Kisa'i is that *inna ma* (إنّما) is a single particle, so it needs no assumed omission, and it is permissible to pause at His saying "*wa-banin*" (وَبَنِينَ). Whoever says that *anna ma* is two particles must have a pronoun returning from the predicate to the subject of *anna* (أنّ), and the pause at "*wa-banin*" is not complete. Al-Sikhtiyani said: it is not good to pause at "*wa-banin*," because *yahsabuna* (يَحْسَبُونَ) "٣٠" requires two objects, and the completion of the two objects is "*fi al-khayrat*." Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 57–60:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive out of fear of their Lord﴾. When He finished mentioning the disbelievers and threatened them, He followed that by mentioning the believers who hasten to good deeds and promised them, and He described them with the most eloquent of their attributes. (Mushfiqun) means fearful and apprehensive of what Allah the Exalted has made them fear.

﴿And those who believe in the signs of their Lord. And those who do not associate anything with their Lord. And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [23:58–60]. Al-Hasan said: "They give with sincerity, and they fear that it will not be accepted from them." Al-Tirmidhi related from ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse, "And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful" [23:60]. ʿAʾisha said: Are they those who drink wine and steal? He said: "No, O daughter of al-Siddiq, but they are those who fast, pray, and give charity, while fearing that it will not be accepted from them. Those are the ones who hasten to good deeds." Al-Hasan also said: "We have met people who were more fearful that their good deeds would be rejected than you are fearful that your sins would be punished for."

ʿAʾisha, Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Nakhaʿi read: "And those who come to what they came [with]" (wa-alladhina ya'tuna ma ata'w), from al-ityan (coming). Al-Farra' said: Even if this reading is authentically from ʿAʾisha, it does not contradict the reading of the majority, because among the Arabs there are those who, in writing hamza, always write an alif in all circumstances. Thus they write sa'ala al-rajul with an alif after the sin, yastahzi'una with an alif between the zay and the waw, and shay'un with an alif after the ya'. So it is not objectionable in their view to write "yu'tuna" with an alif after the ya', and so this word, based on this script, may bear two readings: "yu'tuna ma ata'w" [23:60] and "ya'tuna ma ata'w". The reading of the majority admits of two interpretations. The first: those who give what they have given of zakat and charity while their hearts are fearful. The second: those who give the angels, who record the deeds of the servants, what they have given, while their hearts are fearful. An object has been omitted in this construction because its meaning is clear, as it is omitted in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿In it the people will be given rain, and in it they will press﴾ [Yusuf 12:49], where the meaning is "they press sesame and grapes," and the object was omitted because its interpretation is clear. The original form of the word in its orthography in the Imam (the ʿUthmanic codex) is "ya'tuna," with an alif replacing the hamza, and the alif was written as a waw so that the letters of prolongation and softness would be similar in their hiddenness; this was related by Ibn al-Anbari. Al-Nahhas said: The well-known reading of Ibn ʿAbbas is "wa-alladhina ya'tuna ma ata'w," and it is the reading transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and its meaning is "those who do what they have done," as has been narrated in the hadith. Wajal is close to ishfaq (apprehension) and khawf (fear). The pious and the penitent, their fear concerns the outcome and what will be disclosed to them after death. In His words: ﴿That they are returning to their Lord﴾ [23:60] there is a reminder of the final outcome. In Sahih al-Bukhari: "Actions are only by their endings." As for the one who mixes good and bad deeds, he should be under fear that the threat may be carried out against him because of his mixing. The scholars of the inner states (Ashab al-Khawatir) said: The wajal of the knower regarding his obedience is greater than his wajal regarding his disobedience, because disobedience is erased by repentance, whereas obedience must be sought with the correction of the aim.

(That they) means: because they, or on account of (that they are returning to their Lord) [23:60].

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 23, verse 61:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those hasten to the good things﴾, meaning they hasten to acts of obedience, so that by that they may attain the highest ranks and lofty mansions.

It has been read as "يُسْرِعُونَ" in the good things (*yusri'una*), meaning they are quick to them. "يُسَارِعُونَ" (*yusari'una*) carries the sense of "يُسَابِقُونَ" (*yusabiquna*), that they race those who race them to them, so the object is omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: "يُسَارِعُونَ" is more emphatic than "يُسْرِعُونَ."

﴿And they are foremost in them﴾. The best of what has been said about it is that they get ahead to its appointed times. This indicates that prayer at the beginning of its time is more excellent, as has already been mentioned in *al-Baqarah*. Whoever gets ahead of something has preceded to it, and whoever lags behind it has been outstripped and missed it. So the *lam* in "لَها" (*laha*), according to this view, carries the meaning of "إِلَى" (*ila*, "to"), as in His saying: ﴿بِأَنَّ رَبَّكَ أَوْحى لَها﴾ [Az-Zalzalah: 5], meaning "أوحى إليها" (inspired to it). Sibawayh recited:

*"My she-camel swerves away from the open expanse of al-Yamamah,*
*and she has not aimed, from its people, at anyone other than you."*

[The verse is by al-A'sha. "Tajanuf" means deviation, and "al-jaww" means the wide open expanse.]

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the meaning of ﴿and they are foremost in them﴾, that happiness was decreed for them by Allah, and therefore they hastened to the good things. It was also said: the meaning is "and they, because of the good things, are foremost."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 62:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We do not burden any soul except within its capacity. And with Us is a Book which speaks with truth, and they will not be wronged.﴾ (23:62)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We do not burden any soul except within its capacity.﴾ This has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah [see vol. 3, p. 427], and that it abrogates (naskh) everything in the Sharia that imposes what cannot be borne.

﴿And with Us is a Book which speaks with truth﴾: The most apparent of what has been said about it is that it refers to the Book of Recording of deeds, which the angels raise, and He attributed it to Himself because the angels wrote in it the deeds of the servants by His command. So it "speaks with truth." In this there is a warning and a discouragement of injustice and oppression. The word "speaking" (nutq) may be applied to a book, and the meaning is that the recorders speak by what is in it. And Allah knows best. It was also said that it means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in which everything has been recorded, so they do not go beyond that. It was also said that the reference in His words "And with Us is a Book" is to the Qur'an. Allah knows best, and each is a possibility, but the first is the most apparent.

**Qur'an 23:63–65 in al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this, and they have deeds other than that which they are doing﴾ (23:63) ... ﴿until when We seize their affluent ones with the punishment, behold, they cry out for help﴾ (23:64) ... ﴿Cry not out for help today; surely you will not be helped by Us﴾ (23:65).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾. Mujahid said: that is, in a covering, heedlessness and blindness regarding the Qur'an. It is said: "ghamarahu al-ma'" (the water covered him) when it covered him, and "nahrun ghamr" (a river that covers whoever enters it). And "rajulun ghamr" (a man whom people's opinions overwhelm) [[As in the原 sources. What is in the lexicon books is: "rajul ghamr and ghamr", a man without experience in war or affairs, whom experience has not yet seasoned.]]. It was also said: "ghamrah" because it covers the face, and from this comes "dakhala fi ghimar al-nas wa khimarihim", i.e., into what covers them of the crowd. It was also said: "Nay, their hearts are in confusion" means in bewilderment and blindness, that is, regarding what was described of righteous deeds in the preceding verses; this is the view of Qatadah. Or [it means] regarding the Book that speaks the truth.

(And they have deeds other than that which they are doing) Qatadah and Mujahid said: that is, they have sins which they must commit, apart from the truth. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is, "and they have evil deeds which they have not yet done, other than what they are upon; they must do them apart from the deeds of the believers, and thereby they enter the Fire, because of the wretchedness that has preceded for them." A third possibility is that they wronged creation while disbelieving in the Creator; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The meanings are close to one another.

(Until when We seize their affluent ones with the punishment) meaning with the sword on the day of Badr, said by Ibn Abbas. Al-Dahhak said: meaning with hunger, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar; make for them years like the years of Yusuf." So Allah afflicted them with drought and hunger, until they ate bones, carrion, dogs and carcasses, and wealth and children were destroyed.

(Behold, they cry out for help) that is, they wail and beseech. The root of al-judar is raising the voice in supplication, as a bull does. Al-A'sha describes a cow:

So she circled three times between a day and a night... and the reproach was that she should be loud and bellow.

Al-Jawhari said: al-ju'ar is like al-khuwar; it is said: "ja'ara al-thawr yaju'ur", meaning he cried out. Some reciters read: "'ijlan jasadan lahu ju'ar" (a calf, a body, which has a lowing), related by al-Akhfash. And "ja'ara al-rajul ila Allah 'azza wa jall" means he humbled himself in supplication to Allah. Qatadah said: they shout for repentance, but it is not accepted from them. He said:

He alternates between the prayers of the King... sometimes prostration, and sometimes crying out.

The poet said:

They claimed that they were on the paths of salvation,
but they are only turning back on their heels.

[[In the originals: "innahum" (that they), and the verse does not scan except with the insertion of the letter ba', which here is superfluous, like the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Zaʿama al-ghadaf bi-anna rihlatana ghadan"

Here it is a metaphor for turning away from the truth. Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) read ʿala adbarikum instead of ʿala aʿqabikum, and tankisun with a damma on the kaf.

Abu Raja' read "sumaran," which is the plural of samir, as the poet said:

Do you not see the night-talkers and the people in my condition?

[[This is the second half of a line by Imru' al-Qays. Its first half:

"Faqalat sabaka Allah innaka fadihi"

[ ..... ]]]

In the hadith of Qaylah: "When her husband came from the samir," meaning from the people who converse at night. It is a singular noun with the meaning of a plural, like al-hadir (those who camp by water), and al-baqir (plural of cattle), and al-jamil (plural of camels), both males and females. From it is His saying: ﴿Then We bring you forth as infants﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], meaning as children. It is said: qawm sumr, sumar and samir, and its meaning is staying awake at night, derived from al-samar, which is what falls on trees of moonlight. Al-Jawhari said: al-samir is also al-summar, who are the people who converse at night, just as ḥajj is said for ḥujjaj (pilgrims). The poet's words:

"And a samir in whom play and conversation lasted long"

It is as if he named the place where people gather for conversation after it. It was also said: he used the singular samir while meaning summar, because it was placed in the position of a time, like the words of the poet:

"Other than them, if you come to them at samar, the music of singing-girls and a noisy gathering"

He said samaran because its meaning is: if you come to them at night you will find them conversing. "Ibnā samir" means the night and the day, because conversation takes place in them. It is said: "I will not do it as long as the two sons of samir endure." It is also said: samir means the age, and its two sons are night and day. And "I will not do it as long as the samar and the qamar" means as long as people converse on a moonlit night. And "I will not do it, samir al-layali" (the companion of the nights). Al-Shanfara said:

"There I do not hope for a life that pleases me, the companion of the nights, stripped bare of its crimes"

Al-samar (with a fatha) is thin milk. The Arabs used to sit for conversation, and this made them know the stars, because they sat in the desert and saw the rising stars from the setting ones. The Quraysh used to converse around the Kaʿbah in gatherings for their falsehoods and disbelief, so Allah reproached them for that. And "tahjurun" is read with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the jim, from ahjara, meaning to speak obscenely; and with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the jim, from hajara (the sick man raving) when he delirates. Its meaning: they speak with raving and evil speech about the Prophet (ﷺ) and about the Quran, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and others.

The second: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "Conversation was only disliked when this verse was revealed: ﴿arrogant, conversing by night, talking nonsense﴾," meaning that Allah, Exalted is He, censured people who converse in what is not obedience to Allah, Exalted is He, either in raving or in harming (others). Al-Aʿmash used to say: "If you see a shaykh who has not written down hadith, slap him, for he is one of the shaykhs of the moon," meaning they gather on moonlit nights and talk about the days of the caliphs and the rulers, and none of them knows how to perform wudu' for the prayer.

The third: Muslim narrated from Abu Barzah who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would delay the ʿIshaʾ until a third of the night, and he disliked sleeping before it and conversation after it." The scholars said: As for the dislike of sleeping before it, it is so that it is not exposed to missing its whole time or its best time. For this reason ʿUmar said: "Whoever sleeps, may his eye not sleep," three times. Among those who disliked sleeping before it were ʿUmar, his son ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas and others, and this is the position of Malik. Some permitted it, among them ʿAli, Abu Musa and others, and this is the position of the Kufans. Some stipulated that one should have someone with him to wake him for the prayer. It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar the like of this, and al-Tahawi followed this view. As for the dislike of conversation after it, it is because the prayer has expiated his sins, so he sleeps in safety, and the recording angels have sealed his record with worship. If he converses and talks, he fills it with frivolity and makes its end idle talk and falsehood, and this is not the behavior of believers. Also, conversation tends to lead to overcoming sleep at the end of the night, so he sleeps through the night vigil, and perhaps sleeps through the dawn prayer. It was also said: conversation after it is only disliked because of what Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated, who said the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of conversation after the stillness of the foot, for none of you knows what Allah, Exalted is He, creates of His creation. Close the doors, tie the water-skins, cover the vessels, and extinguish the lamps." It is narrated from ʿUmar that he used to strike people for talking after the ʿIshaʾ, saying: "Conversing at the beginning of the night and sleeping at its end? Give rest to your scribes (recording angels)!" Until it is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: "Whoever composes a line of poetry after the ʿIshaʾ, his prayer will not be accepted until morning." Shaddad ibn Aws traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: the wisdom in disliking conversation after it is only that Allah, Exalted is He, made the night a place of rest (sakan), meaning it is a time for resting in it; so when a person converses in it, he has put it into the day, which is the time of earning a living, as though he intended to oppose Allah's wisdom by which He has established his existence, and so He said: ﴿And He it is who made the night a garment for you, and sleep a rest, and made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan: 47].

The fourth: This dislike applies only to what is not among the acts of nearness, remembrance, and teaching knowledge, or conversing with one's family about knowledge and teaching of benefits and what resembles that. There has come from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from the righteous predecessors (al-salaf) what indicates the permissibility of that, indeed its recommendation. Al-Bukhari said: "Chapter: Conversing about jurisprudence and good after the ʿIshaʾ," and he mentioned that Qurrah ibn Khalid said: "We waited for al-Hasan, and he was late for us until he came close to the time of his standing (prayer). He came and said: 'These neighbors of ours invited us.'" Then Anas said: "We waited for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night until it was midnight; he came, prayed, then addressed us and said: 'The people have prayed, and you have remained in prayer as long as you are waiting for the prayer.'" Al-Hasan said: "Indeed the people are always in good as long as they are waiting for good." He said: "Chapter: Conversing with the guest and the family," and he mentioned the hadith of Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman that the companions of the Suffah were poor... the hadith. Muslim also narrated it. There has come concerning guarding the frontiers and watching the armies at night great reward and immense recompense, as is well known in the reports. Some of that has passed at the end of "Al ʿImran" [see vol. 4, p. 323 onward]. And all praise is due to Allah alone.

Some of that has passed at the end of "Al ʿImran" [see vol. 4, p. 323 onward]. And all praise is due to Allah alone.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not ponder over the Word?﴾ meaning the Qur'an. It is like His saying, exalted is He: "Do they not ponder over the Qur'an?" [[See vol. 5, p. 288 and onward.]] [An-Nisa': 82]. The Qur'an was called "qawl" (word, speech) because they were addressed by it.

﴿Or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ So they denied it and turned away from it. It was also said: "am" here carries the meaning of "bal" (rather), i.e., rather there has come to them that of which their forefathers had no knowledge, and therefore they denied it and abandoned pondering over it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: the meaning is, "Or has there come to them a security from punishment?" and this is something that did not come to their forefathers of old, so they abandoned what was most worthy.

This is a usage the Arabs employ to express rebuke and censure (al-tawqif wa al-taqbih). They say: "Is good more beloved to you, or evil?" meaning: you have been informed of evil, so avoid it. They knew their Messenger and that he was among the people of truthfulness and trustworthiness, so in following him lies deliverance and good, were it not for stubbornness. Sufyan said: "Yes indeed! They knew him, but they envied him!"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 70:

Allah's statement: ﴿Or do they say, "There is madness in him"?﴾ (70). That is, do they argue, in refusing to believe in him, that he is a madman? But he is not like that, because the signs of madness have disappeared from him.

(Nay, he has brought them the truth) (70). That is, the Qur'an, the true Tawhid (Oneness of Allah) and the true religion.

(And most of them) (110). That is, all of them (are averse to the truth) (70), out of envy, transgression and blind imitation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 71:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾. "The truth" here is Allah, glorified and exalted, as said the majority, including Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, Abu Salih and others. Its grammatical construction in Arabic is: "And if the owner of the truth had followed," as said al-Nahhas. It has also been said that it is a metaphor, meaning: if the truth conformed to their desires, so that its conformity to them is called "following" metaphorically; that is, if they were to disbelieve in the messengers and disobey Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and then were not punished or recompensed for that, either through incapacity or ignorance, the heavens and the earth would be corrupted. It has also been said that the meaning is: if the truth were what they claim of taking gods alongside Allah, the gods would conflict, some of them would want what others did not want, the management would be disordered, and the heavens and the earth would be corrupted; and if the two are corrupted, whoever is in them is corrupted. It has also been said: "If the truth had followed their desires," that is, according to what people desire and crave, the order of the world would collapse, because the desires of people differ and oppose one another, whereas the way of the truth is to be followed, and the way of people is to submit to the truth. It has also been said: "the truth" is the Qur'an, meaning: if the Qur'an had come with what they love, the heavens and the earth would be corrupted.

(And whoever is in them) refers to those among them who have intellect: the angels of the heavens and the humans and jinn of the earth, al-Mawardi said. Al-Kalbi said: it means "and whatever is between them of creation," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them would be corrupted." According to al-Kalbi's interpretation and Ibn Mas'ud's reading, the corruption is taken to cover those who have intellect and those who lack it, from animals and inanimate things. The apparent sense of the revelation in the reading of the majority is that it refers to the corruption of those among the animals who have intellect, since what lacks intellect follows what has intellect in goodness and corruption. Accordingly, the corruption that would occur returns to those in the heavens among the angels, in that they would be made lords while they are themselves lorded over, and worshipped while they are themselves made to serve. The corruption of humans takes two forms: first, by following desire, which is destructive; second, by worshipping other than Allah, which is disbelief. As for the corruption of everything else, it occurs by way of consequence, since they are governed by beings endowed with intellect, so the corruption of the governors returns upon them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾, that is, that in which is their honour and their might, as said al-Suddi and Sufyan. Qatadah said: that is, that in which is the mention of their reward and their punishment. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, by the clarification of the truth and the mention of what they need in matters of religion.

﴿But they, from their reminder, are turning away﴾.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 72:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you ask them for any payment?﴾ That is, a wage for what you have brought them. This is the view of al-Hasan and others.

(﴿But the payment of your Lord is better﴾.) Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read "kharajan" with an alif. The rest read it without an alif. All of them read "fakharaju" with an alif, except Ibn 'Amir and Abu Haywah, who read it without an alif. The meaning is: Do you ask them for provision? Then the provision of your Lord is better.

(﴿And He is the best of providers﴾.) That is, no one is able to provide the like of His provision, nor to bestow the like of His bounty. It has also been said: what Allah gives you as reward for your obedience to Him and your calling people to Him is better than the worldly goods they offer. They offered you their wealth, even to the point of making you like the richest man among the Quraysh, but you did not accept that from them. This is the meaning given by al-Hasan. "Al-kharj" and "al-kharaj" are one and the same, except that variation in wording is more elegant; this was said by al-Akhfash. Abu Hatim said: "al-kharj" is a reward or wage, and "al-kharaj" is a gift.

Al-Mubarrad said: "al-kharj" is the verbal noun (masdar), and "al-kharaj" is the noun (ism). Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala about the difference between "al-kharj" and "al-kharaj," and he said: "al-kharaj" is what is obligatory upon you, and "al-kharj" is what you give voluntarily. It is also reported from him that "al-kharj" is [a payment] from slaves, and "al-kharaj" is [a tax] from land. The first was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and the second by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 73–74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path﴾, i.e., to a upright religion. And al-sirat (the path) in the language means the road, so religion is called a path because it leads to Paradise; it is a road to it.

(And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter) (10) i.e., in the Resurrection.

(are deviating from the path) It was said: it is the same as the first. And it was said: they are deviating from the path of Paradise until they arrive at the Fire. Nakaba 'an al-tariq yankubu nukuban means he turned away from it and inclined to something else; and from it comes "nakabat al-rih" (the wind veered) when it did not keep to one course. And the worst of winds is al-nakba'.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 73–74:
