And the worst of winds is al-nakba'.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Even if We had mercy upon them and removed what afflicts them of adversity﴾, meaning: even if We were to return them to the worldly life and did not cause them to enter the Fire, and tested them, [still] they would persist (lalajju) in their transgression (tughyan). Al-Suddi said: "In their disobedience."

(Ya'mahun) Al-A'mash said: they would hesitate (yataraddadun). Ibn Jurayj said: "Even if We had mercy upon them" means in the worldly life, "and removed what afflicts them of adversity," i.e., of drought and hunger, "they would persist" means they would keep going on, "in their transgression" and their misguidance and their overstepping of bounds, "wandering aimlessly" (ya'mahun), meaning they would vacillate and blunder about.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 76:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly seized them with punishment﴾. al-Dahhak said: "With hunger." It was also said: "With illnesses, need and hunger." And it was said: "With killing and hunger."

(﴿But they did not humble themselves before their Lord﴾), that is, they did not submit.

(﴿And they did not supplicate﴾), that is, they did not humble themselves before Allah, mighty and majestic, in the hardships that befell them. Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed concerning the story of Thumamah ibn Uthal, when a raiding detachment (sariyyah) captured him, he embraced Islam, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ released him. He (Thumamah) then cut off the supplies (al-mirah) between Makkah and the Messenger, and said: "By Allah, not a single grain of wheat will come to you from al-Yamamah until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ permits it." Allah then afflicted Quraysh with drought and hunger, until they ate carrion, dogs and al-'ilhiz. It was asked: "What is al-'ilhiz?" He said: They would take wool and fur, moisten it with blood, then roast it and eat it. Abu Sufyan said to him: "I implore you by Allah and by the ties of kinship! Do you not claim that Allah sent you as a mercy to the worlds?" He said: "Yes." He said: "By Allah, I see you have only killed the fathers by the sword, and killed the children by hunger." So there was revealed His statement: "And even if We had mercy upon them and removed what afflicted them of adversity, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 77:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾. Ikrimah said: It is a gate of the gates of Jahannam (Hellfire). Upon it are four hundred thousand of the guardians (al-khazanah), their faces black, their fangs bared, and mercy has been plucked from their hearts. When they reach it, Allah, mighty and majestic, opens it upon them.

Ibn Abbas said: It is their being killed by the sword on the day of Badr.

Mujahid said: It is the famine that struck them, until they ate al-'ilhiz (a kind of blood-and-hide paste) out of hunger, as has been mentioned previously.

It is also said: It is the conquest of Makkah.

﴿Then they will be in it in despair﴾, that is, they will despair, bewildered, not knowing what to do, like one who has given up on relief and on every good.

This has been discussed previously in al-An'am (see vol. 6, p. 426).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾. He made them aware of the abundance of His blessings and the perfection of His power.

(Little is it that you give thanks.) That is, you give thanks only a little. It has also been said: that is, you do not give thanks at all.

The Exalted said: ﴿It is He who produced you on the earth﴾, meaning He brought you into being, dispersed you, and created you.

(﴿And to Him you will be gathered﴾), meaning you will be assembled for recompense.

**Verse 80:** ﴿It is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of the night and the day.﴾

That is, He made them alternate. It is like your saying, "To you is the reward and the gift," meaning that you will be rewarded and given gifts. This is the view of al-Farra' (the grammarian Yahya ibn Ziyad al-Farra'). It has also been said that their alternation is the decrease of one and the increase of the other. It has been said that their alternation is in light and darkness. It has been said that their recurrence is day after night and night after day. A fifth meaning is possible: the alternation, in them, of what has passed of happiness and misery, of misguidance and guidance.

(﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾) to know the reality of His power, His lordship and His oneness, that it is not permissible for Him to have a partner from among His creation, and that He is able to resurrect. Then He reproached them for their words, and informed about them that they (﴿said the like of what the earlier ones said. They said: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we truly be raised?"﴾). This does not happen and cannot be imagined.

(﴿We have indeed been promised this, we and our fathers, before now﴾), that is, before the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ), so we have not seen any reality of it. (﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾), that is, it is nothing but their falsehoods and idle tales. All of this has already been mentioned. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Say﴾), O Muhammad, as a reply to them concerning what they said, (﴿"To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it?"﴾). This informs of His lordship, His oneness, His everlasting dominion, and His power that cannot be changed. So (﴿they will say, "To Allah."﴾), and they must say this. So (﴿Say: "Will you not then remember?"﴾), that is, will you not take heed and know that He who was able to create all of that originally is able to revive the dead after they die?

(﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?" They will say, "To Allah." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾) He means: will you not be afraid, when you attribute to Me what you dislike? You claim that the angels are My daughters, while you dislike daughters for yourselves.

(﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion of all things?"﴾) He means the heavens and what is above them and between them, and the earths and what is beneath them and between them, and what no one knows except Him. Mujahid said: "the dominion of all things" means the treasuries of everything. Al-Dahhak said: the kingdom of everything. The word malakut is an intensive form, like jabarut and rahabut, and it has already been discussed in (al-An'am) [[See vol. 7, p. 23.]].

(﴿He protects, and none can protect against Him﴾), that is, He grants refuge and none can grant refuge against Him. It has also been said: "He protects" means He grants security to whomever He wills, and "none can protect against Him" means that whoever He wills to fear, no one can grant security from Him. Then it has been said: this applies to the world, that is, whoever Allah wills to destroy and to frighten, no preventer will stop Him from him, and whoever He wills to help and to secure, no repeller will repel from him His help and security. It has also been said: this applies to the Hereafter, that is, no preventer will keep Him from one deserving reward, and no repeller will push Him away from one deserving punishment.

(﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾), that is, how are you tricked and turned away from His obedience and His oneness? Or: how is it imagined to you that you associate with Him what neither harms nor benefits? Sihr (magic, deception) is taking-for-imagination (takhyil). All of this is an argument against the Arabs who acknowledged the Creator.

Abu 'Amr recited "Sayaqulun Allah" in the last two places, and this is the qira'ah (recitation) of the people of Iraq. The rest read "Lillah." There is no disagreement that in the first place it is "Lillah," because it is the answer to "Say: To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it?" Since the lam appears in "li-man," it returns in the answer. There is no disagreement that it is written without an alif in all the masahif (codices). As for those who read "Sayaqulun Allah," it is because the question was without a lam, so the answer came in its wording. In the first place, the answer came as "Lillah" because the question had the lam. As for those who read "Lillah" with the lam in the last two places, while there is no lam in the question, it is because the meaning of "Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?" is: "Say: To whom belong the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?" So the answer was "Lillah," since the lam was understood in the question. The reason for the third is the same as the reason for the second.

The poet said:

*When it is said, "Who is the lord of al-Mazalif and the villages,*
*and the lord of the thoroughbred, smooth-coated horses?" I say, "Khalid."*

[[Al-ajrad among horses and animals: the short-haired.]]

That is, "to whom belong the al-mazalif?" [Al-mazalif: al-baraghil, which are the lands between the settled country and the desert; the singular is mazlafah [[from B.]]].

These verses indicate the permissibility of disputing with the disbelievers and establishing the proof against them. This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 3, p. 286.]]. And I have drawn attention to the fact that the one who initiates creation, invention, bringing into existence and originating is the one deserving of divinity and worship.

**Verse 80:** ﴿It is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of the night and the day.﴾

That is, He made them alternate. It is like your saying, "To you is the reward and the gift," meaning that you will be rewarded and given gifts. This is the view of al-Farra' (the grammarian Yahya ibn Ziyad al-Farra'). It has also been said that their alternation is the decrease of one and the increase of the other. It has been said that their alternation is in light and darkness. It has been said that their recurrence is day after night and night after day. A fifth meaning is possible: the alternation, in them, of what has passed of happiness and misery, of misguidance and guidance.

(﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾) to know the reality of His power, His lordship and His oneness, that it is not permissible for Him to have a partner from among His creation, and that He is able to resurrect. Then He reproached them for their words, and informed about them that they (﴿said the like of what the earlier ones said. They said: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we truly be raised?"﴾). This does not happen and cannot be imagined.

(﴿We have indeed been promised this, we and our fathers, before now﴾), that is, before the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ), so we have not seen any reality of it. (﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾), that is, it is nothing but their falsehoods and idle tales. All of this has already been mentioned. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Say﴾), O Muhammad, as a reply to them concerning what they said, (﴿"To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it?"﴾). This informs of His lordship, His oneness, His everlasting dominion, and His power that cannot be changed. So (﴿they will say, "To Allah."﴾), and they must say this. So (﴿Say: "Will you not then remember?"﴾), that is, will you not take heed and know that He who was able to create all of that originally is able to revive the dead after they die?

(﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?" They will say, "To Allah." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾) He means: will you not be afraid, when you attribute to Me what you dislike? You claim that the angels are My daughters, while you dislike daughters for yourselves.

(﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion of all things?"﴾) He means the heavens and what is above them and between them, and the earths and what is beneath them and between them, and what no one knows except Him. Mujahid said: "the dominion of all things" means the treasuries of everything. Al-Dahhak said: the kingdom of everything. The word malakut is an intensive form, like jabarut and rahabut, and it has already been discussed in (al-An'am) [[See vol. 7, p. 23.]].

(﴿He protects, and none can protect against Him﴾), that is, He grants refuge and none can grant refuge against Him. It has also been said: "He protects" means He grants security to whomever He wills, and "none can protect against Him" means that whoever He wills to fear, no one can grant security from Him. Then it has been said: this applies to the world, that is, whoever Allah wills to destroy and to frighten, no preventer will stop Him from him, and whoever He wills to help and to secure, no repeller will repel from him His help and security. It has also been said: this applies to the Hereafter, that is, no preventer will keep Him from one deserving reward, and no repeller will push Him away from one deserving punishment.

(﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾), that is, how are you tricked and turned away from His obedience and His oneness? Or: how is it imagined to you that you associate with Him what neither harms nor benefits? Sihr (magic, deception) is taking-for-imagination (takhyil). All of this is an argument against the Arabs who acknowledged the Creator.

Abu 'Amr recited "Sayaqulun Allah" in the last two places, and this is the qira'ah (recitation) of the people of Iraq. The rest read "Lillah." There is no disagreement that in the first place it is "Lillah," because it is the answer to "Say: To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it?" As for those who read "Sayaqulun Allah," it is because the question was without a lam, so the answer came in its wording. In the first place, the answer came as "Lillah" because the question had the lam. As for those who read "Lillah" with the lam in the last two places, while there is no lam in the question, it is because the meaning of "Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?" is: "Say: To whom belong the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?" So the answer was "Lillah," since the lam was understood in the question. The reason for the third is the same as the reason for the second.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 23, verses 90–92:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But We have brought them the truth﴾ 90. That is, with the true word, not what the disbelievers say, namely the affirmation of a partner and the denial of resurrection.

﴿And indeed, they are liars﴾, in claiming that the angels are daughters of Allah. Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Allah has not taken any offspring﴾. "Min" (from) is *silah* (a redundant particle that adds emphasis without changing the meaning).

﴿And there was not with Him any god﴾. "Min" is *za'idah* (additional). The implied meaning is: Allah has not taken a son as you claim, nor was there a god with Him in what He created. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the meaning is: If there were gods with Him, each god would have independently taken his creation.

﴿And some of them would have overpowered others﴾, that is, the strong would have overcome the weak and sought to dominate them, as is the custom among kings, and a weak, defeated one does not deserve divinity. What indicates the negation of a partner also indicates the negation of a son, because a son would contend with the father for kingship, the way a partner contends.

﴿Exalted is Allah above what they describe﴾, declaring Him free of any son or partner.

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ [i.e. he is [[from B.]] the knower of the unseen]. ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾, a declaration of His transcendence and holiness.

Nafi', Abu Bakr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "*'Alimu*" with a *raf'* (nominative vowel), as *isti'naf* (a resumptive new sentence), meaning: He is the Knower of the unseen. The rest read it with a *jarr* (genitive vowel), as a *sifah* (attribute) of Allah. Ruways related from Ya'qub: "*'Alimi*" with a *khafd* (genitive) when connected in recitation, and "*'Alimu*" with a *raf'* (nominative) when beginning.

He taught him what to supplicate with, meaning: say, "My Lord" — that is, "O my Lord, if You show me what they are promised of the punishment."

(Then do not place me among the wrongdoing people) — that is, in the descent of the punishment upon them; rather, remove me from among them. It has been said: the address (al-nida', "O my Lord") is a parenthetical interjection, and the "mā" in "immā" is superfluous (za'ida). It has also been said: the original of "immā" is "in mā", so "in" is a conditional particle and "mā" is a conditional particle, and the two conditionals were combined for emphasis. The response (jawab) is: "then do not place me among the wrongdoing people," meaning: if You intend to punish them, then remove me from among them.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, knew that Allah, exalted is He, would not place him among the wrongdoing people when the punishment descended upon them, yet the Lord commanded him with this supplication and request so that his reward would be magnified and so that he would be mindful of his Lord, exalted is He, at all times.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 96:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Repel evil with that which is better﴾. This is a command to pardon and to noble character. Whatever of it pertains to this community in their dealings among themselves is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) and remains in force for the community forever. As for what pertains to dealing peacefully with the disbelievers (muwada'ah), leaving off confronting them, and overlooking their affairs, it is mansukh (abrogated) by fighting (al-qital).

﴿We are best aware of what they describe﴾, i.e., of their associating partners with Allah and their denial. This indicates that the verse is one of peaceful disengagement (muwada'ah), and Allah knows best.

The Qur'an, 23:97–98: "And say: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whispers (hamazat) of the devils."

There are two issues here.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from the whispers (hamazat) of the devils﴾. The *hamazat* is the plural of *hamzah*. In the lexicon, *al-hamz* means prodding and pushing. It is said: *hamazahu*, *lamazahu* and *nakhasahu*, meaning he pushed him. Al-Layth said: *al-hamz* is speech from behind the nape, and *al-lamz* is speech delivered face to face. The devil whispers and murmurs his suggestion into the chest of the son of Adam. This is His saying, "I seek refuge in You from the whispers of the devils," meaning the devils' prods that distract from the remembrance of God, Exalted is He. In a hadith: "He used to seek refuge from the *hamz* of the devils, their *lamz*, and their *hams*." Abu al-Haytham said: when one speaks secretly and conceals his speech, that is *al-hams* (murmuring) of speech. The lion is called *hawس* (*hawsa*, a stealthy name), because it moves lightly, so the sound of its footfall is not heard. This has already been discussed in (the commentary on) Surah Ta-Ha.[[See vol. 11, p. 247.]]

**The second issue:** God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers to seek refuge from the Satan in his *hamazat*, which are the fits of anger in which a person does not control himself. It seems these are what afflict believers alongside the unbelievers, when hostility occurs, and that is why this verse is connected to it. The *nazghat* (incitements) and the surges of anger that come from the Satan are what is sought refuge from in the verse. This has already been fully explained at the end of Surah al-A'raf,[[See vol. 7, p. 347.]] and also in the introduction to this book.[[See vol. 1, p. 86.]]

It was narrated from Ali ibn Harb ibn Muhammad al-Ta'i: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Hibban, that Khalid used to be troubled with sleeplessness at night. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he commanded him to seek refuge with the perfect words of God from the wrath and punishment of God, from the evil of His servants, from the *hamazat* of the devils, and from ﴿that they attend me﴾.

In the book of Abu Dawud, Umar said: "And their *hamz* is *al-mawtah*." Ibn Majah said: *al-mawtah* means madness. Seeking refuge from madness is also a concern (of this verse).

In the reading (qira'a) of Ubayy: "My Lord, seeking refuge in You from the *hamazat* of the devils, and seeking refuge in You ﴿that they attend me﴾," meaning that they be with me in my affairs. For when they attend a person, they are prepared for *hamz*, and when they are not present, there is no *hamz*.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the Satan attends one of you at every matter of his affairs, to the extent that he attends at his food. So when a morsel falls from one of you, let him remove whatever harm is on it, then eat it, and let him not leave it for the Satan. And when he finishes, let him lick his fingers, for he does not know in which of his food the blessing lies."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 99–100:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back!"﴾ The discourse returns to mentioning the polytheists, meaning: they said, "When we are dead..." up to His saying, "These are nothing but the fables of the ancients." Then He argued against them and reminded them of His power over everything. Then He said: they persist in that until, when death comes to one of them, he becomes certain of his misguidance and sees the angels who seize his soul, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the lives of those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Anfal: 50]. [[See vol. 8, p. 28.]]

(He says, "My Lord, send me back!") He wishes for a return so that he may act righteously in what he left behind. The saying may also be within the self, as God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And they say within themselves, "Why does God not punish us for what we say?"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 8]. As for his saying "send me back" (irji'uni), while he is addressing his Lord, mighty and majestic, and did not say "send me back" in the singular (irji'ni), it came in the form of honouring the one addressed (plural of respect). It was also said: they first called upon God, mighty and majestic, and then one of them said, "My Lord," then he turned to addressing the angels and said, "Send me back" (irji'una) to the world; this was related by Ibn Jurayj. It was also said that the meaning of "irji'una" is by way of repetition, i.e., "send me back, send me back, send me back," and so on. Al-Muzani said concerning His saying, ﴿Cast into Hell﴾ [Qaf: 24], that it means "cast, cast." Al-Dahhak said: the intended ones are the people of polytheism. I say: the request for return is not restricted to the disbeliever, for a believer may also ask for it, as at the end of Surat al-Munafiqun, as will come. The verse indicates that no one dies until he knows by necessity whether he is among God's friends or among God's enemies; and were it not so, he would not ask for a return, for they would know that before the descent of death and its taste.

(That I may act righteously) [23:100]. Ibn Abbas said: he means "I bear witness that there is no god but God."

(In what I have left behind) [23:100], i.e., in what I neglected and left off acting upon of acts of obedience. It was also said: "in what I have left behind" [23:100] refers to wealth, so that I may give charity. And "la'alla" (perhaps) implies uncertainty, whereas this one who asks for a return has become certain of the punishment, and he is resolving himself to righteous deeds without any uncertainty. The uncertainty thus refers either to his being returned to the world, or to success, i.e., "I will act righteously if You grant me success," since he is not certain of having the ability and success were he returned to the world.

(Never!) [23:100] This is a word of refusal, meaning: the matter is not as he supposes, that he will be granted a return to the world; rather, it is a statement that is blown away by the winds. It was also said: even if he were granted what he asks, he would not fulfil what he says, as He said: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28] [[See vol. 6, p. 10.]]. It was also said: ﴿It is a word he is saying﴾ [23:100] refers to God, may He be exalted, meaning there is no discrepancy in His report, and He has reported that He will not delay a soul when its term comes, and He has reported that this disbeliever will not believe. It was also said: ﴿It is a word he is saying﴾ [23:100] at the time of death, but it will not benefit him.

(Behind them is a barrier) [23:100], i.e., in front of them and before them. It was also said: behind them. "Barzakh" [23:100] means a barrier between death and resurrection; this was said by al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. It is also related from Mujahid that the barzakh is the barrier between death and returning to the world. From al-Dahhak: it is what lies between this world and the Hereafter. Ibn Abbas: a screen. Al-Suddi: a term. Qatadah: the remainder of the world. It was also said: a respite until the Day of Resurrection, related by Ibn Isa. Al-Kalbi: it is the term between the two blasts, and between them is forty years. These sayings are close to one another. Every barrier between two things is a barzakh. Al-Jawhari said: the barzakh is the barrier between two things. The barzakh is what lies between this world and the Hereafter, from the time of death until resurrection; so whoever dies has entered the barzakh. A man in the presence of al-Sha'bi said: "May God have mercy on so-and-so, for he has become one of the people of the Hereafter!" He said: "He has not become one of the people of the Hereafter, but he has become one of the people of the barzakh, and he is neither of this world nor of the Hereafter." And "yawm" (day) is attached to "yub'athun" (they are resurrected) because it is a temporal adverb, and the intended meaning of the attachment is the verbal noun.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 23, verse 101:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the Trumpet is blown﴾. What is meant by this blowing is the second blast.

(﴿So there will be no kinship ties between them that day, nor will they ask about one another﴾.) Ibn 'Abbas said: They will not boast of their lineages in the Hereafter as they boast of them in this world, and they will not ask one another in the Hereafter as they ask in this world, "From which tribe are you?" or "Of what lineage are you?" And they will not recognise one another because of the terror that has overwhelmed them.

It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that this refers to the first blast, when whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills. "So there will be no kinship ties between them that day, nor will they ask about one another." Then another blast will be blown, and behold, they will be standing, looking on. Then some of them will turn to others, asking one another.

A man asked Ibn 'Abbas about this verse and His saying: ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 50]. He said: They will not ask one another at the first blast, because no living being will remain on the earth, so there will be no lineages and no questioning. As for His saying, ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 50], this refers to when they enter Paradise, and then they will ask one another.

Ibn Mas'ud said: This verse refers only to the second blast.

Abu 'Umar Zadhan said: I entered upon Ibn Mas'ud and found that the people of goodness and the people of the right had got there before me. So I called out at the top of my voice: "O 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud! Because I am a non-Arab, you have brought these people near and kept me away!" He said: "Come closer." So I drew near, until there was no one sitting between me and him, and I heard him say: "On the Day of Resurrection a servant or a maidservant will be taken by the hand and set up before the first and the last. Then a herald will call out: 'This is so-and-so, son of so-and-so. Whoever has a right against him, let him come to his right.' The woman will rejoice when a right is owed to her from her father, her husband, her brother or her son." Then Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿So there will be no kinship ties between them that day, nor will they ask about one another﴾. "Then the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, will say: 'Give these people their rights.' He will say: 'O Lord, the world has perished, so from where shall I give them?' The Lord will say to the angels: 'Take from his good deeds and give every person according to the measure of his claim.' If he was a friend of God, and there remains of his good deeds the weight of a mustard seed, God will multiply it until He admits him to Paradise by it." Then Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong [even] the weight of an atom. And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa': 40]. "But if he was wretched, the angels will say: 'Lord! His good deeds are exhausted, and claimants remain.' God, exalted, will say: 'Take from their deeds, add them to his evil deeds, and write out for him a certificate to Hell.'"
The discussion of them has already been given.
The discussion of them has already been given.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Fire scorches their faces﴾ [23:104]. It is also said "tanfahu" (تَنْفَحُ), with the same meaning, and from it: ﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord touches them﴾ [al-Anbiya: 46][[See vol. 11, p. 292 onward.]]. However, "talfahu" is more forceful in harm. It is said: the fire and the scorching wind (samum) "lafahathu" (scorched him) with its heat, meaning it burned him. And "lafahtuhu bil-sayf lafhatan" means I struck him with the sword with a light blow[[As in the lexicographical works. In the manuscripts it reads "ḍarabtuhu ḥaqīqah" (I struck him in reality), which is a distortion.]].

(﴿and they therein are grimacing﴾) [23:104]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "frowning" (ʿābisūn). The lexicographers said: al-kulūḥ is a baring of the teeth with a scowl, and al-kālih is one whose lips have drawn back and whose teeth are exposed. Al-Aʿmash said:

"To him is the forefront, with no like of it, at the time the cheek drew back from the tooth, grimacing."

The man "kalaḥa" (grimaced) "kulūḥan" and "kilāḥan." How ugly his grimace is, referring to the mouth and what surrounds it. A "dahr kālih" is a harsh age. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "﴿and they therein are grimacing﴾" means like one who has grimaced, whose lips have drawn back and whose pus has flowed. Ibn Masʿud said: Have you not seen the head scorched by the fire, its teeth exposed and its lips shriveled?

In al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said regarding ﴿and they therein are grimacing﴾: "The fire scorches him so that his upper lip shrinks until it reaches the middle of his head, and his lower lip hangs down until it strikes his navel." He said: This is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 23, verses 106–108:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people who went astray."﴾ ١٠

The recitation of the people of Medina, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim is "شِقْوَتُنا" (shiqwatunā) ١٠. The Kufans, except 'Asim, recited "شَقَاوَتُنَا" (shaqāwatunā). This recitation is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan. It is said: "شَقَاءٌ" (shaqā') and "شَقًا" (shaqan), with the long and short vowel. The best of what has been said about its meaning is: our desires and our appetites overcame us. He called the desires and appetites "شِقْوَة" (shiqwah, wretchedness), because they lead to it, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [An-Nisa': 10], because that leads them to the Fire. It has also been said: it is what was preceded in Your knowledge and written against us in the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab) of wretchedness. It has also been said: it is a good opinion of oneself and a bad opinion of others.

(﴿and we were a people who went astray﴾) ١٠ That is, we were astray from guidance in our actions. This is not an excuse from them; rather it is an acknowledgment. This is shown by their saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then we are wrongdoers﴾ ١٠. They sought a return to the world, as they had sought it at death. "فَإِنْ عُدْنا" (if we return) ١٠ to disbelief, "فَإِنَّا ظالِمُونَ" (then we are wrongdoers) ١٠ against ourselves by returning to it. Then they are answered after a thousand years: (﴿Remain in it, and do not speak to Me﴾) ١٠. That is, be removed far away in Hell, as one says to a dog: "اخْسَأْ" (ukhsa', be gone), meaning go far away. "خَسَأْتُ الْكَلْبَ خَسْئًا" means I drove the dog away. "خَسَأَ الْكَلْبُ" by itself, "خُسُوءًا", is used both transitively and intransitively. "انْخَسَأَ الْكَلْبُ" is also used.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: He said: Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah narrated to us from Qatadah, who related it from Abu Ayyub, from Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: The people of Hell call upon Malik, and he does not answer them for forty years. Then he replies to them: "Indeed you are remaining." He said: By Allah, their supplication to Malik and the Lord of Malik was worthless. He said: Then they call upon their Lord and say: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people who went astray. Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then we are wrongdoers﴾ ١٠ - ١٠٦. He said: Then He keeps silent toward them for the length of two lifetimes of the world. He said: Then He answers them: "Be gone into it." He said: By Allah, the people did not utter a word after it, and there was nothing but the groaning and sobbing of the Fire of Hell. So their voices were likened to the voices of donkeys: the beginning of it is groaning (zafir) and its end is sobbing (shahiq). Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it as marfu' (traced back to the Prophet) with a similar meaning, from Abu al-Darda'.

Qatadah said: The voice of the disbelievers in the Fire is like the voice of a donkey, its beginning is groaning and its end is sobbing. Ibn 'Abbas said: They will produce a barking like the barking of dogs. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: It reached me, or it was mentioned to me, that the people of the Fire cried out for help to the guardians (al-khazanah)... the report in its entirety, which Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned. We have mentioned it in full in al-Tadhkirah, and at its end: Then He remained away from them for as long as Allah willed, then He called out to them: ﴿Were not My verses recited to you, and you denied them?﴾ ١٠ He said: When they heard His voice, they said: "Now our Lord will have mercy on us." At that they said: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us" ١٠, that is, the decree which was written against us, "and we were a people who went astray. Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then we are wrongdoers" ١٠ - ١٠٦. Then He said at that: "Be gone into it, and do not speak to Me" ١٠. At that, the supplication and the hope came to an end. Some of them turned toward others, barking in each other's faces, and they were enveloped.

(﴿and we were a people who went astray﴾) ١٠ That is, we were astray from guidance in our actions. This is not an excuse from them; rather it is an acknowledgment. This is shown by their saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then we are wrongdoers﴾ ١٠. They sought a return to the world, as they had sought it at death. "فَإِنْ عُدْنا" (if we return) ١٠ to disbelief, "فَإِنَّا ظالِمُونَ" (then we are wrongdoers) ١٠ against ourselves by returning to it. Then they are answered after a thousand years: (﴿Remain in it, and do not speak to Me﴾) ١٠. That is, be removed far away in Hell, as one says to a dog: "اخْسَأْ" (ukhsa', be gone), meaning go far away. "خَسَأْتُ الْكَلْبَ خَسْئًا" means I drove the dog away. "خَسَأَ الْكَلْبُ" by itself, "خُسُوءًا", is used both transitively and intransitively. "انْخَسَأَ الْكَلْبُ" is also used.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: He said: Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah narrated to us from Qatadah, who related it from Abu Ayyub, from Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: The people of Hell call upon Malik, and he does not answer them for forty years. Then he replies to them: "Indeed you are remaining." He said: By Allah, their supplication to Malik and the Lord of Malik was worthless. He said: Then they call upon their Lord and say: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people who went astray. Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then we are wrongdoers﴾ ١٠ - ١٠٦. He said: Then He keeps silent toward them for the length of two lifetimes of the world. He said: Then He answers them: "Be gone into it." He said: By Allah, the people did not utter a word after it, and there was nothing but the groaning and sobbing of the Fire of Hell. So their voices were likened to the voices of donkeys: the beginning of it is groaning (zafir) and its end is sobbing (shahiq). Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it as marfu' (traced back to the Prophet) with a similar meaning, from Abu al-Darda'.

Qatadah said: The voice of the disbelievers in the Fire is like the voice of a donkey, its beginning is groaning and its end is sobbing. Ibn 'Abbas said: They will produce a barking like the barking of dogs. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: It reached me, or it was mentioned to me, that the people of the Fire cried out for help to the guardians (al-khazanah)... the report in its entirety, which Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned. We have mentioned it in full in al-Tadhkirah, and at its end: Then He remained away from them for as long as Allah willed, then He called out to them: ﴿Were not My verses recited to you, and you denied them?﴾ ١٠ He said: When they heard His voice, they said: "Now our Lord will have mercy on us." At that they said: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us" ١٠, that is, the decree which was written against us, "and we were a people who went astray. Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then we are wrongdoers" ١٠ - ١٠٦. Then He said at that: "Be gone into it, and do not speak to Me" ١٠. At that, the supplication and the hope came to an end. Some of them turned toward others, barking in each other's faces, and they were enveloped.

**The Qur'an, 23:109–111** (the passage is from al-Qurtubi's commentary, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said, "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us"﴾ [23:109], and so on to the end of the verse. Mujahid said: They were Bilal, Khabbab, Suhayb, and so-and-so and so-and-so, from among the weak Muslims. Abu Jahl and his companions used to ridicule them.

﴿But you took them in mockery﴾ [23:110]. It is read with a *damma* (ḍamma) on the sin (*sukhriyyan*, pronounced *sukhriyyan*) here, and in Sad [see vol. 15, p. 224 onward], by Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i. The rest read it with a *kasra* (*sikhriyyan*). Al-Nahhas said: Abu 'Amr distinguished between the two readings, taking the *kasra* to mean ridicule (*tahazzu'*) and the *damma* to mean subjugation (*sukhrah*). Khalil, Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' did not recognize this distinction. Al-Kisa'i said: They are two dialects with the same meaning, as one says *ʿisiyyun* and *ʿusiyyun*, and *lujjiyyun* and *lijjiyyun*. Al-Tha'labi related from al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' the distinction mentioned by Abu 'Amr, that the *kasra* means mockery and ridicule by speech, while the *damma* means subjugation and making subservient by action. Al-Mubarrad said: Distinctions in meaning are taken from the Arabs, but as for interpretation (*ta'wil*), it does not arise from this. The *kasra* in *sikhriyyan* carries both meanings together, because the *damma* is considered heavy in such a form.

﴿Until they made you forget My remembrance﴾ [23:110]; that is, you were so busy ridiculing them that you forgot My remembrance.

﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾ [23:110], mocking them. He attributed the causing of forgetfulness to the believers, because they were the cause of the disbelievers being occupied away from His remembrance. The evil consequence of their mockery of the believers extended to the disbelief taking control of their hearts.

﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience﴾ [23:111], for their endurance of your harm, and for their patience in obeying Me.

﴿That they are the triumphant﴾ [23:111]. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *innahum* with a *kasra* on the *hamza*, as the beginning of praise from Allah the Exalted for them; the rest read it with a *fatha*, meaning "because they are the triumphant." It may also be read in the accusative, as the object of the reward falling upon it, its sense being: "I have rewarded them today with the triumph of Paradise." I say: The meaning of this may be compared with the words of Allah the Exalted at the end of al-Mutaffifin: ﴿Today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ [83:34], through to the end of the surah, as its explanation will come there, God willing [see vol. 19, p. 265 onward].

From this is derived: a warning against mocking, ridiculing, belittling and disparaging the weak and the needy, and occupying oneself with them in matters that bring no benefit; and that such conduct distances one from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verses 112–114:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said, "How many years did you remain on the earth?"﴾ It was said: this means in the graves. It was also said: this is a question to them about the length of their lives in the world. This question is put to the polytheists in the plains of Resurrection or in the Fire.

﴿The number of years﴾ is read with a fatha on the nun (*nūn*), treating it as a sound masculine plural (*jam' musallam*). Some Arabs read it with a kasra and tanwin (*yakhfiduhā wa yunawwinuhā*).

﴿They said, "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ The severity of the punishment made them forget the length of their stay in the graves. It was also said that the punishment was lifted from them between the two blasts (*nafkhatayn*, the two blasts of the Trumpet), so they forgot what they had suffered in their graves. Ibn 'Abbas said: the punishment they had endured from the first blast until the second made them forget. This is because whoever was killed by a prophet, or killed a prophet, or died in the presence of a prophet, was punished from the moment of death until the first blast. Then the punishment is withheld from him, and it becomes like water until the second blast is sounded. It was also said that they regarded the length of their stay in the world and in the graves as short, compared with what they were now facing.

﴿So ask those who count.﴾ That is, ask the reckoners who know this, for we have forgotten it. Or ask the angels who were with us in the world. The first view is the saying of Qatadah, and the second is the saying of Mujahid.

Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿Say, "How many years did you remain on the earth?"﴾ in the imperative. This reading may bear three meanings. First: "Say, 'How many years did you remain?'" The speech takes the form of a command addressed to one person, but it is meant for the group, since the meaning is understood. Second: it is a command to the angel to ask them on the Day of Resurrection about the length of their stay in the world. Third: it means, "Say, O disbelievers, how many years did you remain?" The rest read ﴿He said, "How many years..."﴾ in the declarative form, meaning that Allah the Exalted said to them, or that the angels said to them, "How many years did you remain?"

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i also read ﴿Say, "You remained only a little"﴾ in the imperative. The rest read ﴿He said﴾ (30) in the declarative form, according to the first interpretation mentioned. The meaning is: you did not remain on the earth except a little. This is because their stay in the graves, however long it was, was finite. It was also said that it is little compared with their stay in the Fire, because that has no end.

﴿If only you had known.﴾ That is, that.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 115:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose?﴾ That is, left neglected, as cattle are created with no reward for them and no punishment upon them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36], meaning, like the cattle, left idle without any benefit. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim, Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Ali, said: Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, created the creation as slaves so that they would worship Him, and He rewards them for worship and punishes them for abandoning it. If they worship Him, then today they are free, noble slaves of His, freed from the bondage of this world, kings in the abode of Islam; and if they reject servitude, then today they are runaway, base, despicable slaves, and tomorrow they are enemies in the prisons, among the layers of the fires.

And "'abathan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) according to Sibawayh and Qutrub. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is in the accusative as an absolute object (masdar), or because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

(And that you will not be returned to Us) so that you will be recompensed for your deeds. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "turja'un" (tarji'un) with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the jim, from al-ruju' (return).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 116:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth﴾ [23:116]. That is, Allah, the King, the Truth, is far removed and sanctified above children, partners and equals, and above creating anything in vain or foolishly, because He is al-Hakim (the All-Wise).

﴿There is no deity except Him, the Lord of the Noble Throne﴾ — there is nothing else in the Qur'an like it. Ibn Muhaysin read, and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir, "al-Karim" in the nominative (bi-l-raf') as a description of Allah [[In Ruh al-Ma'ani: "al-Karim" in the nominative, as a description of the Lord, and it is permitted that it be a description of the Throne by way of cutting off (qat')."]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 23, verse 117–118:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof﴾, meaning, he has no argument for it. (﴿Then his account is only with his Lord﴾), meaning, He will punish him and call him to account. "Innahu" (the hā' is the pronoun of the matter and the affair, al-amr wa al-sha'n) ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah recited "lā yufliḥu" with a fatḥah, meaning: from those who denied and rejected what I brought and were ungrateful for My blessing.

Then He commanded His Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, to seek forgiveness, so that the community might follow his example. It was also said: He commanded him to seek forgiveness for his community.

Al-Tha'labi narrated with a chain (isnad) from the hadith of Ibn Lahi'ah, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Hubayrah, from Hanash ibn ʿAbd Allah al-San'ani, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud, that he passed by a afflicted man who was being tested, and he recited into his ear: "Did you think that We created you in vain?" until he finished the surah, and he was cured. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (What did you recite into his ear?) So he informed him, and he said: (By Him in whose hand my soul is, if a man with certainty recited it upon a mountain, it would move).
